teile.einleitung: The Kopaonik is a mountain range in the south of Serbia. The largest ski area in the country is there. Part of the mountains is also protected as a national park.
wichtigste: The Kopaonik lies in the south of Serbia.
It is the largest ski area in Serbia.
The highest peak is over 2000 metres high.
Part of the mountains is a national park.
In summer hikers and cyclists come.

abschnitte.titel: A mountain range in the south of Serbia
abschnitte.text: The **Kopaonik** is one of the largest mountain ranges in **Serbia**. It lies in the south of the country, close to the border with Kosovo. The highest peak is called **Pančićev vrh** and is a little over 2000 metres high. It is named after the naturalist Josif Pančić, who studied the plants of Serbia.

On the Kopaonik lies the **largest ski area in Serbia**. In winter there is a lot of snow there and numerous pistes and chairlifts. Many people from Serbia and the neighbouring countries spend their **winter holidays** there. In summer hikers and mountain bikers come.

Part of the mountains has been a **national park** since 1981. Dense coniferous forests and rare plants grow there, some of which occur only in this area. Many species of bird also live in the park. The protection is meant to help nature survive despite tourism.

gewusst: On the highest peak stands the tomb of Josif Pančić, after whom the peak is named.

teile.einleitung: Paella is a well-known rice dish from Spain. It comes from the area around Valencia and is named after the flat pan in which it is cooked.
wichtigste: Paella is a Spanish rice dish.
It comes from the area around Valencia, where rice has been grown for a long time.
In Valencian “paella” simply means “pan”.
Saffron makes the rice yellow.
Paella valenciana includes chicken, rabbit and green beans.
The crispy layer at the bottom is called socarrat.

abschnitte.text: **Paella** is a dish of **rice**, with vegetables, meat or seafood added. The name comes from **Valencian** and simply means **“pan”**. So the dish is named after its large, flat pan with two handles. Because the pan is so flat, the rice lies in only a thin layer.

Paella comes from the area around **Valencia** on the east coast of Spain. **Rice** has been grown there for a long time, for example in the fields around the Albufera lagoon. Traditionally paella is cooked outdoors over an **open wood fire**. The wood gives the rice a light **smoky flavour**.

The real **paella valenciana** is cooked with **chicken** and **rabbit**. Added to this are **green beans** and olive oil. The spice **saffron** colours the rice yellow and gives it flavour. Saffron is one of the most expensive spices in the world. In **paella de marisco**, on the other hand, go seafood such as **mussels**, **prawns** and squid.

A paella is not stirred once the rice is in the pan. At the bottom it turns lightly brown and **crispy**. This layer is called the **socarrat** and for many people is the best part of the paella. In Spain paella is often eaten at weekends with the whole family, sometimes straight from the pan.

gewusst: Paella is traditionally eaten at midday rather than in the evening.
For festivals, giant paellas are sometimes cooked in pans several metres across.

teile.einleitung: The Hebrides are a group of many islands in the Atlantic off the west coast of Scotland. They are known for wild landscapes, seabirds, the Gaelic language and Harris Tweed. A distinction is made between the Inner and the Outer Hebrides.
wichtigste: The Hebrides lie off the west coast of Scotland.
A distinction is made between the Inner and Outer Hebrides.
The Isle of Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides.
Since 1995 a bridge has led to Skye.
On the Outer Hebrides many people speak Scottish Gaelic.
Harris Tweed is woven there by hand.
St Kilda was abandoned by its last inhabitants in 1930.

abschnitte.text: The Hebrides consist of hundreds of islands, but only a small number of them are inhabited. The **Inner Hebrides** lie close to the Scottish mainland. They include Skye, Mull, Islay and Jura. The **Outer Hebrides** lie further out in the Atlantic. The largest island there is Lewis and Harris, and there are also North Uist, South Uist and Barra, for example. Ferries link the islands with the mainland.

The **Isle of Skye** is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides. It has steep mountains, rock pinnacles and cliffs by the sea. Since 1995 it has been linked to the mainland by the **Skye Bridge**. Before that you could only get there by ferry. Today Skye is one of the most popular destinations in Scotland.

On the Outer Hebrides, **Scottish Gaelic** is spoken more than anywhere else in Scotland. This old Celtic language is related to Irish. Place signs are often bilingual. The islands are also famous for **Harris Tweed**, a sturdy woollen cloth. It is woven by hand in people's homes, and only cloth woven that way on the Outer Hebrides may carry this name.

The island group of **St Kilda** lies far out in the Atlantic. People lived here for a long time in great isolation, mainly on seabirds, sheep and a little farming. In 1930 the last inhabitants were taken to the mainland at their own request. Today the islands are home mainly to huge colonies of **seabirds** such as gannets and puffins. St Kilda is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

On the small island of **Iona**, the Irish monk Columba founded a monastery in the 6th century. From there Christianity spread in Scotland. Later the Vikings ruled the Hebrides for a long time. On the island of **Islay** there are now several well-known whisky distilleries. On the island of Staffa lies **Fingal's Cave**, whose walls are made of basalt columns.

gewusst: Fingal's Cave inspired the composer Felix Mendelssohn to write a famous piece of music, the Hebrides Overture.
On the Outer Hebrides there are white sandy beaches that recall the Caribbean, although the water is cold.

teile.einleitung: Latvia is one of the three Baltic states on the Baltic Sea. Its capital Riga is famous for its many Art Nouveau buildings. Latvia belongs to the EU and has paid with the euro since 2014.
wichtigste: Latvia lies in the middle between Estonia in the north and Lithuania in the south.
Riga was founded in 1201 and is famous for its Art Nouveau.
The Daugava, in German the Düna, flows into the Baltic Sea at Riga.
Jūrmala has over 30 kilometres of sandy beach.
Latvia joined the EU in 2004 and introduced the euro in 2014.
Gauja National Park is also called “Livonian Switzerland”.

abschnitte.titel: In the middle of the Baltics
abschnitte.text: The three **Baltic states** are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. **Latvia** lies in the middle: in the north it borders **Estonia**, and in the south **Lithuania**. In the west lies the **Baltic Sea**. The region in the west on the coast is called **Courland**, in Latvian Kurzeme, with ports such as Liepāja and Ventspils. Other historic regions are Livonia, Semigallia and Latgale.

**Riga** was founded in **1201** by Bishop **Albert of Buxhoeveden**. Later the city became a member of the **Hanseatic League**, an alliance of trading cities. Since 1997 the old town has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Through Riga flows the **Daugava**, which flows into the **Gulf of Riga**.

Riga has one of the largest collections of **Art Nouveau buildings** in the world. **Art Nouveau** is a style of building from around the year 1900 with curving lines, plants and faces on the façades. A large part of the buildings in the centre date from this time. Many of them were designed by the architect **Mikhail Eisenstein**.

West of Riga lies the seaside resort of **Jūrmala** on the Gulf of Riga. It has over **30 kilometres of sandy beach** and is known for old wooden villas and spa baths. In the east, around Sigulda, lies **Gauja National Park**, founded in 1973 and the oldest national park in Latvia. Because of its hills, sandstone cliffs and castles, travellers called the area **“Livonian Switzerland”**.

Latvia joined the **European Union** in **2004**. On **1 January 2014** it replaced its currency, the **lats**, with the **euro**. As the capital, Riga is also the largest city in the country. Latvia is also known for its great **song and dance festivals**, at which thousands sing together.

gewusst: One area in Latvia is called “Livonian Switzerland” because it reminded travellers of Switzerland.
Riga has more Art Nouveau buildings than hardly any other city in the world.

teile.einleitung: Germany is a federal state and consists of 16 Länder, which are also called federal states. Each Land has its own government and a capital. This is similar to the cantons in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Germany has 16 federal states.
Bavaria is the largest Land, at about 70,500 square kilometres.
North Rhine-Westphalia has the most inhabitants.
Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen are city states.
Saarland is the smallest of the area states.
The capital of Hesse is Wiesbaden, and of Lower Saxony it is Hanover.

abschnitte.text: Germany is a **federal state**. It consists of **16 Länder**, which are called **federal states**. Each Land has its own parliament, the **Landtag**, and its own **state government**. The Länder decide, for example, on schools and police. This recalls the **cantons** of Switzerland, which also manage many tasks themselves.

**Bavaria**, at about **70,500 square kilometres**, is the largest Land in Germany. That makes it larger than the whole of Switzerland. **North Rhine-Westphalia** has the most inhabitants, with about 18 million people. It is densely populated and has many large cities. The smallest **area state** is **Saarland**, at about 2,570 square kilometres. It borders France and Luxembourg.

A **city state** is a city that is also a federal state of its own. In Germany there are three of them: **Berlin**, **Hamburg** and **Bremen**. The Land of Bremen even consists of two cities: **Bremen** and the port city of **Bremerhaven** at the mouth of the Weser. Between them lies territory belonging to Lower Saxony.

The largest city of a Land is not always the capital. In **Hesse** **Frankfurt am Main** is the largest city, but the state capital is **Wiesbaden**. The capital of **Lower Saxony** is **Hanover** on the River Leine, known for its large trade fair. Right in the north lies **Schleswig-Holstein** between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. It borders **Denmark**.

gewusst: Bavaria alone is larger than the whole of Switzerland.
Between the two cities of the Land of Bremen lies another federal state.

teile.einleitung: Europe has many large cities with millions of inhabitants. Which city is the largest depends on how you count: only within the city limits, or with all the suburbs. The figures here are rough guides from the 2020s.
wichtigste: Moscow is the largest city that lies entirely in Europe.
Within its city limits, Berlin is the largest city in the EU.
Within its narrow city limits, Paris has only about 2 million inhabitants.
Stockholm is the most populous city in Scandinavia.
Valletta on Malta is the smallest capital of an EU country.
Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland, ahead of Geneva and Basel.

abschnitte.text: The largest city that lies entirely in Europe is **Moscow**, with about 13 million inhabitants. **Istanbul** is even bigger, but lies partly in Asia. In the **European Union**, **Berlin** is the largest city within its city limits, with just under 4 million people. **London**, with about 9 million, is also one of the largest cities in Europe.

The city of **Paris** has only about 2 million inhabitants, although more than 12 million people live in the wider area. The reason is that the **city limits** are drawn very tightly. The municipality of Paris covers only about **105 square kilometres**. Most people in the **metropolitan region** live in suburbs outside this boundary. That is why cities are often compared by their whole urban area as well.

In Italy, **Rome** is the largest city, with just under 3 million inhabitants, and **Milan** follows as the second largest and is the economic centre. In Scandinavia, **Stockholm** is the largest, with almost a million inhabitants. The city is built on **14 islands**. The smallest capital of an EU country is **Valletta** on Malta, with only about 5,000 to 6,000 inhabitants. It was built as a fortress city in the 16th century.

Compared with the rest of Europe, Swiss cities are rather small. The largest is **Zurich**, with over 440,000 inhabitants. Zurich is not the capital, however: the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament is **Bern**. In second place comes **Geneva** with about 200,000 inhabitants, followed by **Basel** in third place.

gewusst: At about 105 square kilometres, the municipality of Paris is smaller than the canton of Zug.
Valletta has fewer inhabitants than many Swiss villages and is still a capital.

teile.einleitung: The Kaliningrad Oblast is a region of Russia on the Baltic Sea that has no land link to the rest of Russia. Its capital, Kaliningrad, was formerly called Königsberg and has a long German history.
wichtigste: Kaliningrad lies on the Baltic Sea between Poland and Lithuania.
Because it is cut off from the motherland, it is called an exclave.
Until 1946 the city was called Königsberg and was the capital of East Prussia.
The philosopher Immanuel Kant was born in Königsberg in 1724.
In the region lie about 90 per cent of the known amber deposits in the world.
In Baltiysk lies the main base of the Russian Baltic Fleet.

abschnitte.text: The Kaliningrad Oblast borders **Poland** and **Lithuania** on land and the **Baltic Sea** in the west. It has no land link with the Russian heartland. An area that is cut off from its state in this way is called an **exclave**. An **enclave**, by contrast, would be entirely surrounded by a single foreign state. Since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Lithuania and Belarus lie between Kaliningrad and Russia.

**Königsberg** was for centuries a German city and the capital of **East Prussia**. After the Second World War it came under Soviet administration in **1945**. In **1946** it was renamed after the Soviet politician **Mikhail Kalinin**. The German population had to leave the region, and people from the Soviet Union moved here.

The philosopher **Immanuel Kant** was born in Königsberg in **1724**. He taught at the university and is buried at the cathedral. Also famous is the puzzle of the **seven bridges of Königsberg**. The Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** proved in **1736** that you cannot cross all the bridges exactly once and return. In doing so he founded **graph theory**.

**Amber** is fossilised tree resin. Near **Yantarny** it is extracted by open-cast mining from old layers of earth. In the region lie about **90 per cent** of the known amber deposits in the world. The **Curonian Spit**, a long narrow spit of land with high dunes, is shared by Kaliningrad with Lithuania. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In **Baltiysk**, formerly Pillau, lies the main base of the Russian **Baltic Fleet**. The port is ice-free in winter. Between Kaliningrad and Belarus lies the **Suwałki Gap**, a border strip only about 65 kilometres wide between Poland and Lithuania. It is regarded as a strategically sensitive spot. In 2022 Poland opened a **canal** through the Vistula Spit, so that ships to Elbląg no longer have to pass through the Russian strait.

gewusst: For Euler's bridge problem, all that matters is how the bridges are connected, not how long they are.
Kant is said to have almost never left Königsberg.

teile.einleitung: Cappadocia is a landscape in central Anatolia in Turkey. It is famous for its pointed rock towers, cave churches and underground cities. Early in the morning, many hot air balloons often float over the land.
wichtigste: Cappadocia lies on a high plateau in central Anatolia, south-east of Ankara.
The rocks consist mainly of soft volcanic tuff.
The pointed rock towers are called fairy chimneys.
Derinkuyu is an underground city with many levels.
In the Göreme Open Air Museum there are churches carved out of the rock.
Since 1985 the region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: A very long time ago, volcanoes such as **Erciyes** covered the land with thick layers of ash. This turned into a soft rock, **tuff**. Wind and water wore the soft stone away over a long time. Where a harder cap of rock lay on top, a column was left standing beneath it. This is how the **fairy chimneys** formed, pointed towers with a hat of stone.

Because tuff is easy to hollow out, people dug homes into the rock from an early date. Christian **monks** carved churches and monasteries into the rock walls. Many are painted with coloured **wall paintings**. In the **Göreme Open Air Museum** you can visit many of these rock churches.

In Cappadocia there are several **underground cities**. The best known is **Derinkuyu**. It reaches many levels deep into the ground and offered protection to thousands of people. There were stables, kitchens, storerooms and **ventilation shafts**. Large round stones could close off the passages.

Cappadocia is a popular travel destination. At sunrise, often over a hundred **hot air balloons** rise above **Göreme**. The calm morning air makes these flights possible. Since **1985** Göreme National Park and the rock sites have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, as both a natural and a cultural heritage site.

gewusst: Some of the cave dwellings in Cappadocia are now hotels, where you can spend the night in a rock room.
It stays cool in the tuff even in the hot summer, which is why fruit and potatoes are still stored there today.

teile.einleitung: High-speed trains run on special lines at 250 kilometres per hour or more. In Europe they link big cities so quickly that they can often keep up with aeroplanes. Well-known examples are the TGV, the ICE and the Frecciarossa.
wichtigste: The high-speed train of France is called the TGV.
From 1981 the first TGV line linked Paris and Lyon.
In 2007 a TGV set a world record at about 575 km/h.
In Germany the ICE trains of Deutsche Bahn run.
Spain has the longest high-speed network in Europe.
The Eurostar runs through the Channel Tunnel from London to Paris.
The TGV Lyria links Switzerland with Paris.

abschnitte.text: Under **EU** rules, newly built railway lines count as **high-speed lines** if trains can run on them at at least 250 km/h. Upgraded old lines count from about 200 km/h. Lines like these have wide curves, few gradients and no level crossings. The trains are built to be especially streamlined. The first high-speed railway in the world was the Shinkansen in Japan in 1964.

**TGV** stands for “train à grande vitesse”, which means a high-speed train. From **1981** the first line ran from **Paris to Lyon**. It was the first high-speed line in Europe and shortened journey times greatly. In normal service the TGV runs at up to 320 km/h. On 3 April 2007 a modified TGV reached 574.8 km/h. To this day that is the **world record** for trains with wheels on rails.

In Germany the fast trains are called **ICE**, which stands for Intercity-Express. They run on new lines at up to 300 km/h and also reach Basel and Zurich. In Italy the **Frecciarossa**, which means “red arrow”, runs at up to 300 km/h. **Spain** has built a very large network since 1992, which at almost 4,000 kilometres is the longest in Europe. The lines link Madrid with many big cities.

The **Eurostar** runs from London to Paris and Brussels. On the way it passes through the **Channel Tunnel**, which is about 50 kilometres long and runs under the English Channel. Since 1994 the tunnel has linked England with France. Before that you had to cross the Channel by ship or aeroplane. Today the journey from London to Paris takes only a little over two hours.

Switzerland is linked to its neighbouring countries by fast trains. The **TGV Lyria** runs from Zurich, Basel, Geneva and Lausanne, among other places, to Paris. From Basel the journey takes only about three hours. In Switzerland itself, there is less emphasis on very high speed and more on a dense **regular-interval timetable** with good connections. The **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, however, makes fast journeys through the Alps possible.

gewusst: In the 2007 record run, the TGV travelled faster than many small aeroplanes fly.
At about 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

teile.einleitung: Corsica is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean. It lies off the coast of Italy, but has belonged to France since 1768. In French it is called the “Île de Beauté”, the island of beauty.
wichtigste: Corsica has belonged to France since 1768.
The capital is Ajaccio on the west coast.
Napoleon Bonaparte was born on Corsica in 1769.
The highest mountain is Monte Cinto at 2706 metres.
The Strait of Bonifacio separates Corsica from Sardinia.
As well as French, people speak Corsican, which is related to Italian.
The long-distance footpath GR 20 crosses the island.

abschnitte.titel: A mountain range in the sea
abschnitte.text: Corsica is mostly **mountainous**, with high mountains and deep valleys. That is why the island is also called a mountain range in the sea. The highest mountain is **Monte Cinto** in the north, which is 2706 metres high. In the south the **Strait of Bonifacio** separates Corsica from the Italian island of Sardinia. This strait is only about 11 kilometres wide.

For a long time Corsica was ruled by the city republic of **Genoa**. In the **Treaty of Versailles of 1768**, Genoa gave the island to France. Since then Corsica has belonged to France. The capital is **Ajaccio** on the west coast. Marseille, Nice and Toulon, on the other hand, lie on the French mainland.

The most famous Corsican is **Napoleon Bonaparte**. He was born in Ajaccio in 1769, shortly after Corsica had become French. Later he became **Emperor of the French** and conquered large parts of Europe. With the Act of Mediation of 1803 he also gave Switzerland a new order. In Ajaccio you can visit his birthplace.

As well as French, people on Corsica speak **Corsican**. This language is closely related to **Italian**. Many place signs are bilingual. The polyphonic singing, the **polyphony**, is also well known. Many Corsicans are proud of their own history and culture.

The long-distance footpath **GR 20** crosses Corsica from north to south. It is about 180 kilometres long and leads through the mountains. It is regarded as one of the most demanding hiking trails in Europe. Many hikers from Switzerland also take on the route. On the way you stay overnight in simple mountain huts.

gewusst: After Sicily, Sardinia and Cyprus, Corsica is the fourth largest island in the Mediterranean.
From Bonifacio in the south you can see across to Sardinia in clear weather.

teile.einleitung: The Vltava is the longest river that runs entirely within the Czech Republic. It flows through Prague and became known through a famous piece of music by Bedřich Smetana.
wichtigste: In German the Vltava is called the Moldau.
It rises in the Bohemian Forest in the south-west of the Czech Republic.
It is about 430 kilometres long and flows entirely through the Czech Republic.
Near Mělník it flows into the Elbe.
In Prague the Charles Bridge crosses the Vltava.
Bedřich Smetana dedicated the piece of music “Vltava” to it.

abschnitte.text: The Vltava, in German the **Moldau**, rises in the **Bohemian Forest** in the south-west of the Czech Republic, near the border with Germany. At first it flows through forests and moors. Soon it is dammed to form the large **Lipno Reservoir**, the largest lake in the Czech Republic. After that it winds through the beautiful old town of **Český Krumlov**.

The Vltava flows north through **Bohemia**. On the way there are several reservoirs that generate electricity. The Vltava is about **430 kilometres** long and so the longest river that runs entirely within the Czech Republic. Near the town of **Mělník** it flows into the **Elbe**, in Czech Labe. The Elbe flows on through Germany to the North Sea.

In the capital, **Prague**, the Vltava flows right through the old town. Many bridges cross it. The best known is the **Charles Bridge** from the 14th century with its statues. High above the river stands **Prague Castle**. In 2002 the Vltava burst its banks after heavy rain and flooded parts of the city.

In the 19th century the composer **Bedřich Smetana** wrote the cycle **“My Country”**. One part of it is called **“Vltava”**. The music tells the course of the river: from two small springs through forests and fields to Prague. You hear splashing water, a hunt and a peasant wedding. The piece is also often heard in Swiss schools in music lessons.

gewusst: At the start of Smetana's piece you hear two flutes, which represent the two source streams of the Vltava.
Although the Vltava is longer than the Elbe up to their confluence, the river is called the Elbe after that.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has five neighbouring states: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. At the borders there are exciting special features such as tripoints and exclaves.
wichtigste: Switzerland's neighbours are Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
Switzerland has its longest border with Italy.
In Basel Switzerland, Germany and France meet.
On Lake Constance Switzerland, Germany and Austria border each other.
Büsingen is a German exclave, and Campione d'Italia an Italian one.
Liechtenstein is the only neighbour not in the EU.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland borders **Germany** in the north, **Austria** and **Liechtenstein** in the east, **Italy** in the south and **France** in the west. It has its longest border with **Italy** and the shortest with Liechtenstein. Four of the five neighbours belong to the **European Union**. Only **Liechtenstein** is not in the EU, but is a member of the European Economic Area.

At the **Dreiländereck**, the tripoint in the Rhine harbour of **Basel**, Switzerland, Germany and France meet. There stands a monument that juts out into the Rhine. On **Lake Constance** too there are shores of three countries: Switzerland, Germany and Austria. Exactly how the border runs through the lake has **never been fixed** to this day.

An **exclave** is a piece of land that is completely surrounded by the territory of another state. **Büsingen am Hochrhein** is a German municipality in the middle of the canton of **Schaffhausen**. There people mostly pay with **Swiss francs**. **Campione d'Italia** is an Italian municipality on **Lake Lugano** that is completely surrounded by Ticino territory.

The canton of **Geneva** is largely surrounded by **France**. Only by a narrow strip is it linked to the canton of Vaud and so to the rest of Switzerland. Every day many people travel from France to Geneva to work. They are called **cross-border commuters**.

Switzerland is particularly closely tied to **Liechtenstein**. Since 1923 the two countries have formed a shared **customs area**, and in Liechtenstein people pay with the **franc**. With its EU neighbours Switzerland has many **treaties**, for example on trade and travel. Because Switzerland belongs to the **Schengen area**, there are mostly no passport checks at the borders.

gewusst: Switzerland's border is almost 2000 kilometres long in total.
In Büsingen some Swiss rules apply, for example for customs, although it belongs to Germany.

teile.einleitung: The Grossglockner is the highest mountain in Austria. It belongs to the Alps and lies in the Hohe Tauern National Park. At its foot lies the largest glacier in the country.
wichtigste: At 3798 metres, the Grossglockner is the highest mountain in Austria.
It lies in the Hohe Tauern National Park.
The summit lies on the border between Carinthia and Tyrol.
At its foot lies the Pasterze, the largest glacier in Austria.
In 1800 people stood on the summit for the first time.
The Grossglockner High Alpine Road was opened in 1935.

abschnitte.text: The **Grossglockner** is **3798 metres** high, so almost 3800 metres. It is the highest mountain in **Austria** and much higher than any mountain in Germany. It belongs to the **Alps**, just like the high mountains of Switzerland. The summit lies on the border between **Carinthia** and **East Tyrol**, which belongs to Tyrol. On the top stands a **summit cross** made of metal.

At the foot of the Grossglockner lies the **Pasterze**, the largest **glacier** in Austria. A glacier is a slowly flowing river of ice. Because of **global warming**, the Pasterze gets smaller every year. The same is seen with Swiss glaciers such as the Aletsch Glacier.

The Grossglockner is the highest peak in the **Hohe Tauern National Park**, the largest national park in the Alps. Ibexes, chamois and eagles live here. On the mountain meadows, **marmots** live in burrows in the ground. If one sees an eagle, it warns the others with a loud **whistle**.

In **1800** a group of mountaineers reached the summit for the first time. Today the Grossglockner is a popular goal for experienced alpinists. Since **1935** the **Grossglockner High Alpine Road** has led across the Alps close to the mountain. It links the state of Salzburg with Carinthia and is closed in winter because of snow.

gewusst: Marmots warn each other of danger with a shrill whistle.
The Grossglockner High Alpine Road can only be driven in the summer half of the year.

teile.einleitung: Munich is the capital of the German federal state of Bavaria and lies on the Isar. The city is known for the Oktoberfest, Marienplatz and large museums.
wichtigste: Munich is the capital of Bavaria in the south of Germany.
The Isar flows through Munich.
The Oktoberfest is one of the largest folk festivals in the world.
In the centre lies Marienplatz with the New Town Hall.
The Frauenkirche has two towers with round domes.
The English Garden is one of the largest city parks in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Munich** is the capital of the federal state of **Bavaria** in the south of Germany. After Berlin and Hamburg it is the third largest city in Germany. Through the city flows the **Isar**, on whose banks many people lie in the sun in summer. From Switzerland Munich is easy to reach, for example by train from Zurich.

**Marienplatz** is the centre of the old town. There stands the **New Town Hall** with a tall tower. In the tower there is a **glockenspiel**, in which colourful figures turn and dance to music. Not far from it stands the **Frauenkirche** with its **two towers** and round domes, a landmark of the city.

The **Oktoberfest** is one of the largest folk festivals in the world. It already begins in **September** and lasts a good two weeks. There are festival tents, fairground rides and music, and many visitors wear traditional costume. The first festival took place in **1810**, when a Bavarian crown prince married.

The **English Garden** is one of the largest city parks in the world, even larger than Central Park in New York. In the park there are meadows, streams and beer gardens. In the south of the city on the Isar lies the zoo **Hellabrunn**. Animals from all over the world live there.

The **Deutsches Museum** is one of the largest **museums of technology** in the world. It lies on an island in the Isar. There you can see aeroplanes, ships, old machines and even a replica **mine**. Many experiments you may try out yourself.

gewusst: In the English Garden people surf on a standing wave in the Eisbach, in the middle of the city.
Munich lies closer to the Alps than any other large German city, and when the foehn blows you can see the mountains.

teile.einleitung: Ostrog Monastery is a Serbian Orthodox monastery in Montenegro. It was built high up in an almost vertical rock face. It is one of the most important places of pilgrimage in the Balkans.
wichtigste: Ostrog Monastery lies in Montenegro.
It was built in the 17th century into an almost vertical rock face.
It was founded by Saint Basil of Ostrog.
It is an important place of pilgrimage.
The monastery is visited by people of different religions.

abschnitte.text: **Ostrog Monastery** lies inland in **Montenegro**, between the towns of Podgorica and Nikšić. The upper monastery was built in the **17th century** directly into an almost **vertical rock face**. From far away it looks as if the white building is stuck to the rock. Small churches are set up in caves in the rock.

The monastery was founded by **Basil of Ostrog**, a bishop of the Serbian Orthodox Church. After his death he was venerated as a **saint**. His mortal remains are kept in the monastery. Many people come to pray there and to ask for help.

Ostrog is one of the best-known **places of pilgrimage** for Orthodox Christians. Every year very many **pilgrims** visit it, and some walk up the steep path on foot. Muslims and Catholics also come to the monastery. Below lies the lower monastery, which was built later.

gewusst: The upper monastery lies about 900 metres above sea level, high above the valley of the River Zeta.

teile.einleitung: The North Cape is a high cliff in the far north of Norway. Many people take it for the northernmost point of Europe, and every year numerous visitors come there.
wichtigste: The North Cape lies on the island of Magerøya in Norway.
The cliff rises about 307 metres steeply out of the sea.
It lies at about 71 degrees north.
Its landmark is a globe made of steel.
Knivskjellodden lies about 1.5 kilometres further north.
The seafarer Richard Chancellor gave it the name “North Cape” in 1553.

abschnitte.text: The **North Cape** lies on the island of **Magerøya** in the region of Finnmark in Norway. A **tunnel** under the sea links the island with the mainland. The North Cape lies at about **71 degrees north**. For comparison: the **Arctic Circle** lies at about 66.5 degrees north, and Switzerland at about 46 to 48 degrees.

The North Cape is a **rock plateau** that rises about **307 metres** steeply out of the sea. From above you look out over the **Arctic Ocean**. On the plateau stands a **globe made of steel**, the landmark of the North Cape. Almost all visitors take a photograph there. In summer the Sun does not set here for weeks, which is called the **midnight sun**.

Although many believe it: the North Cape is not the northernmost point of the island. The headland of **Knivskjellodden** lies about **1.5 kilometres** further north. It can only be reached on foot, however, and is therefore less well known. Because Magerøya is an island, the northernmost point of the European **mainland** lies at yet another place.

In **1553** the English seafarer **Richard Chancellor** sailed past the cliff. He was looking for a sea route to **Asia** by way of the north. He called the cliff **“North Cape”**. Later more and more travellers came to see this special place.

gewusst: At the North Cape there are weeks in winter when the Sun does not rise at all.
The North Cape Tunnel descends more than 200 metres below sea level.

teile.einleitung: Pirin National Park lies in the mountain range of the same name in the south-west of Bulgaria. It is known for glacial lakes, limestone peaks and ancient forests and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The Pirin Mountains lie in the south-west of Bulgaria.
Pirin National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
There are many glacial lakes there.
The highest peak is Vihren.
Many peaks consist of limestone or granite.

abschnitte.text: The **Pirin Mountains** lie in the south-west of **Bulgaria**, between the rivers Struma and Mesta. Their highest peak is **Vihren**, at a good 2900 metres. That makes it, after Musala, the second highest mountain in Bulgaria. Many peaks consist of pale **limestone**, others of granite.

In the ice age there were **glaciers** in the Pirin. They dug hollows in the rock in which many clear **glacial lakes** now lie. In the forests grow old pines and firs. Animals such as bears, wolves and chamois live there.

A large part of the mountains is protected as a **national park**. Since **1983** it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. At the edge of the park lies the town of **Bansko**, a well-known winter sports resort. In summer many hikers come to the mountains.

gewusst: In the Pirin stands one of the oldest pine trees in Europe, the Baikushev Pine, which is said to be over 1000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Korčula is an island in Croatia on the Adriatic coast of Dalmatia. The town of the same name has a well-preserved medieval old town. It claims to be the birthplace of the traveller Marco Polo.
wichtigste: Korčula is an island in Croatia in the Adriatic.
The town of Korčula has a medieval old town with town walls.
Korčula claims to be the birthplace of Marco Polo.
This cannot be proved, and Venice is often named as well.
The island belonged for a long time to the Republic of Venice.

abschnitte.text: **Korčula** lies in the **Adriatic** off the coast of **Dalmatia** in the south of Croatia. The island is green, with pine forests, olive groves and vineyards. The town of the same name lies on a small peninsula. Its old town is surrounded by **walls** and towers, and the lanes are laid out like a fishbone.

**Marco Polo** was a merchant from **Venice** who travelled as far as China in the 13th century. A famous book came out of his journey. The town of Korčula claims he was born there, and shows a house that is said to have belonged to him. This cannot be **proved**, and Venice is often named as his birthplace too. What is certain is that the island then belonged to the sphere of power of Venice.

Korčula is also known for the **Moreška**, an old **sword dance**. In it two groups of dancers fight over a woman in a play. The dance is performed mainly in summer for visitors. It is an important part of the island's culture.

gewusst: The name Korčula goes back to the ancient Greeks, who called the island “Black Corcyra” because of its dark forests.

teile.einleitung: The Hardangervidda is a huge high plateau in the south of Norway. It is regarded as the largest high plateau in Europe. There are hardly any trees here, but countless lakes, streams, bogs and large herds of wild reindeer.
wichtigste: The Hardangervidda lies in southern Norway.
It is regarded as the largest high plateau in Europe.
It mostly lies at a height of about 1100 to 1300 metres.
The largest herds of wild reindeer in Europe live there.
A large part of it is protected as a national park.

abschnitte.titel: Wide land above the tree line
abschnitte.text: The Hardangervidda is a wide, gently rolling plateau. It mostly lies at a height of about 1100 to 1300 metres. That is so high and so far north that hardly any trees grow there. Instead there are lichens, mosses, dwarf shrubs, and many **lakes** and **bogs**. The weather can change quickly, and it can snow even in summer. In the west lies the glacier **Hardangerjøkulen**.

The largest herds of **wild reindeer** in Europe live on the Hardangervidda. Reindeer are well adapted to the cold: they have a thick coat and broad hooves, so they do not sink into the snow. In winter they scrape the snow away to reach the **lichens** underneath. To protect the animals and the landscape, a large part of the plateau was declared a **national park** in 1981.

The Hardangervidda is a popular area for hiking and, in winter, for cross-country skiing. There is a network of simple huts where you can stay overnight. On the northern edge, the **Bergen Line** runs from Oslo to Bergen across the highlands. The station of **Finse** is one of the highest stations in Norway. Anyone out and about there must be well equipped, because the paths lead through lonely country.

gewusst: Scenes for a well-known Star Wars film were shot near Finse, because the landscape looks like an ice planet.
The Hardangervidda is about one fifth the size of the whole of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Kinnarodden is a cape in the far north of Norway. It is the northernmost point of the European mainland. Many people think of the North Cape here, but that lies on an island.
wichtigste: Kinnarodden is the northernmost point on the European mainland.
The cape lies on the Nordkinn peninsula in Norway.
The North Cape and Knivskjellodden lie on the island of Magerøya.
Kinnarodden lies a little east of the North Cape.
No road leads to the cape.

abschnitte.text: Kinnarodden lies in the province of **Finnmark** in the north of **Norway**, far north of the Arctic Circle. It is the tip of the **Nordkinn** peninsula. The cape is the northernmost point that you can reach on the European **mainland**. In summer the Sun does not set there for weeks, and in winter it stays dark for a long time.

The famous **North Cape** lies on the island of **Magerøya**, as does the headland **Knivskjellodden**, which reaches a little further north. Because both lie on an island, they do not count as mainland. Kinnarodden lies a little further east. The North Cape is easy to reach by road and tunnel and is therefore much better known.

**No road** leads to Kinnarodden. You can only reach the cape by a long **hike** through wild, rocky terrain or by boat. That is why only a few visitors get there. The area is rough and windy and almost without trees.

gewusst: The North Cape is more famous, but Kinnarodden is the real record holder on the mainland.

teile.einleitung: At about 1000 kilometres, the Loire is the longest river in France. Its valley is famous for magnificent castles and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
wichtigste: The Loire is about 1000 kilometres long, the longest river in France.
It rises at Mont Gerbier de Jonc in the Massif Central.
Near Saint-Nazaire it flows into the Atlantic.
In the Loire Valley stand many castles, such as Chambord and Chenonceau.
Since 2000 the Loire Valley has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In 1429 Joan of Arc helped to liberate Orléans.

abschnitte.text: The Loire rises at **Mont Gerbier de Jonc**, an old volcanic cone in the département of Ardèche in the Massif Central. At first it flows north, then in a great arc to the west. It flows through towns such as **Orléans**, Blois, Tours and **Nantes**. Near **Saint-Nazaire** it flows into the Atlantic. Its whole course of about 1000 kilometres lies in France.

Mainly in the 15th and 16th centuries, kings and nobles built magnificent **castles** in the Loire Valley. The largest is **Chambord**, which King Francis I had built. It has a famous double spiral staircase: two people can go up and down at the same time without meeting. The castle of **Chenonceau** stands on arches over the Cher, a tributary of the Loire, almost like a bridge.

The artist and inventor **Leonardo da Vinci** spent the last years of his life in **Amboise** on the Loire. He died there in 1519. Earlier still, in 1429, **Joan of Arc** helped to liberate the city of Orléans, which was under siege in the Hundred Years' War. That is why she is also called “the Maid of Orléans”.

In 2000 **UNESCO** declared a large part of the Loire Valley a World Heritage Site. Not only individual castles are protected, but the whole landscape with towns, vineyards and villages. The Loire is regarded as one of the most natural large rivers in western Europe. It has many sandbanks, and its water level varies greatly.

The mild climate in the Loire Valley is well suited to fruit, vegetables and wine. That is why the area is also called the **Garden of France**. Many well-known wines bear the names of places on the Loire. Every year very many visitors cycle along the river from castle to castle.

gewusst: On the spiral staircase of Chambord two people can walk at the same time and see each other without meeting.
The Loire flows through France only along its whole length and crosses no national border.

teile.einleitung: Monaco is a tiny country on the Mediterranean coast and, after the Vatican, the second smallest state in the world. It is a principality, famous for its casino, Formula 1 and a large marine museum.
wichtigste: Monaco is a principality and is ruled by a prince.
Since 2005 Albert II has been the prince (as of 2025).
The Grimaldi family has ruled Monaco since the Middle Ages.
On land Monaco borders only France.
People pay with the euro, although Monaco does not belong to the EU.
The flag is red at the top and white at the bottom.
Every year Formula 1 races through the streets.

abschnitte.text: Monaco is a **principality**: at the head of the state stands a **prince**. Since 2005 this has been **Albert II** (as of 2025). He comes from the **Grimaldi** family, which has ruled Monaco since the Middle Ages. The colours of the family, **red and white**, are also the colours of the flag. In front of the **Prince's Palace** on the rock, the **changing of the guard** takes place every day shortly before noon, and many tourists watch it.

Monaco is only about **2 square kilometres** in size, so smaller than some Swiss municipalities. On the land side it is completely surrounded by **France**, and on the other side lies the **Mediterranean**. Because there is so little space, many tall buildings stand close together. Monaco is one of the most densely populated countries in the world.

In the **Monaco Grand Prix** Formula 1 cars race through narrow streets, bends and even a **tunnel**. The race is regarded as one of the most famous in the world. A well-known district is called **Monte Carlo**. There stand a magnificent **casino** and many luxury hotels.

The **Oceanographic Museum** stands on a rock right above the sea. It was founded by Prince Albert I, who was very interested in marine research. In the large **aquarium** you can see fish, corals and many other sea creatures. For a long time the well-known French marine explorer Jacques-Yves Cousteau directed the museum.

In Monaco people pay with the **euro**. The country is not a member of the **European Union**, but has an agreement with it. That is why Monaco is even allowed to mint its own **euro coins**. These coins are very sought after by collectors, because there are only a few of them.

gewusst: Monaco is so small that you can walk across it in about an hour.
The flag of Monaco looks almost the same as the flag of Indonesia, only the proportions are slightly different.

teile.einleitung: Niš is one of the largest cities in Serbia and lies in the south of the country. In Roman times it was called Naissus and was the birthplace of Emperor Constantine the Great.
wichtigste: Niš lies in the south of Serbia on the River Nišava.
In Roman times the city was called Naissus.
Here in the 3rd century Emperor Constantine the Great was born.
Constantine promoted Christianity in the Roman Empire.
In the middle of the city stands a large fortress.

abschnitte.text: The **Romans** already had a city here, called **Naissus**. It lay on an important road that ran right across the Balkans. In the **3rd century AD** **Constantine the Great** was born here. He later became Roman emperor. Outside the city the remains of a Roman palace complex are preserved.

**Constantine the Great** is among the most important Roman emperors. He allowed **Christians** to practise their faith freely and promoted **Christianity**. He also founded the city of **Constantinople**, today's Istanbul. Niš is proud of its famous son to this day.

Today **Niš** is one of the largest cities in **Serbia**. It lies on the River **Nišava**, not far from where it flows into the South Morava. In the middle of the city stands a large **fortress** from Ottoman times. In the park inside the walls concerts take place in summer.

gewusst: In 2013 Niš celebrated the 1700th anniversary of the Edict of Milan, which is linked with Constantine.

teile.einleitung: Every country in Europe has a capital. That is usually where the government has its seat, and often it is also the largest city in the country. Here you can get to know some important capitals and what makes them special.
wichtigste: London is the capital of Great Britain, and Dublin is the capital of Ireland.
Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.
Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands.
The Baltic states have Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius as their capitals.
Reykjavík is the northernmost capital of an independent state.
Stockholm is built on 14 islands.
Nicosia in Cyprus has been divided since 1974.

abschnitte.text: A **capital** is the most important city of a country. That is usually where the **government** and the **parliament** sit. Switzerland is a special case: Bern is officially not a capital, but the **federal city**. The Federal Council and Parliament meet there. The capital is also not always the largest city: in Switzerland, Zurich is bigger than Bern.

abschnitte.titel: The British Isles and the Netherlands
abschnitte.text: **London** on the Thames is the capital of Great Britain. The United Kingdom also includes Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The capital of Scotland is **Edinburgh**, and an old castle stands high above the city. The Republic of Ireland has **Dublin** as its capital, while Belfast lies in Northern Ireland. **Amsterdam** is the capital of the Netherlands and is known for its canals and bicycles.

**Reykjavík** in Iceland lies at about 64 degrees north. It is the northernmost capital of an independent state. **Stockholm**, the capital of Sweden, lies where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea, and is built on 14 islands. The three **Baltic states** also have capitals on or near the Baltic Sea: **Tallinn** in Estonia, **Riga** in Latvia and **Vilnius** in Lithuania.

**Ljubljana** is the capital of Slovenia, a small country that borders Italy and Austria. **Sarajevo**, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, lies in a valley surrounded by mountains. On the island of Cyprus lies **Nicosia**. Since 1974 this capital has been divided by a ceasefire line into a Greek Cypriot part and a Turkish Cypriot part. The line is monitored by UN troops.

The smallest capital is also a whole state: **Vatican City** in Rome. It is the smallest state in the world. **Andorra la Vella** in the Pyrenees is regarded as the highest capital in Europe. The largest capitals include **Moscow**, **London** and **Paris**. Many capitals lie on rivers, for example Paris on the Seine, and Vienna and Budapest on the Danube.

gewusst: The Danube flows through four capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
Vienna and Bratislava are only about 60 kilometres apart. Only Rome and Vatican City lie even closer together.

teile.einleitung: Naples is a large city in the south of Italy on the Bay of Naples. Above it rises the volcano Vesuvius, and it is regarded as the home of pizza.
wichtigste: Naples is the capital of the region of Campania.
After Rome and Milan, Naples is the third largest city in Italy.
Vesuvius lies only about 10 kilometres away, and its last eruption was in 1944.
The pizza Margherita is said to have originated in Naples in 1889.
The name comes from the Greek “Neapolis”, meaning “new city”.
Off the coast lies the island of Capri with the Blue Grotto.

abschnitte.text: **Naples** was founded by **Greek settlers**. They called the city **“Neapolis”**, meaning **“new city”**. In Italian this became **Napoli**, and in English Naples. Today Naples is the capital of the region of **Campania** and, after Rome and Milan, the **third largest city** in Italy. The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

On the Bay of Naples rises **Vesuvius**, only about **10 kilometres** from the city. It is an active **volcano**. In **AD 79** an eruption buried the Roman cities of **Pompeii** and Herculaneum under ash. The last eruption was in **1944**. Researchers now watch the volcano closely.

Naples is regarded as the home of **pizza**. The **pizza Margherita** is said to have been baked in **1889** in honour of Queen **Margherita**. Tomato, mozzarella and basil recall the colours of the Italian flag: red, white and green. UNESCO counts the art of the Neapolitan pizza makers as intangible cultural heritage.

In the bay lies the island of **Capri**. Famous is its **Blue Grotto**, a sea cave in which the water glows deep blue through the incoming sunlight. South of Naples lies the **Amalfi Coast** with steep rocks and colourful places such as **Positano** and **Amalfi**. It too is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Under Naples there is a huge network of tunnels and caves that the ancient Greeks already dug.
The famous footballer Diego Maradona played for SSC Napoli for several years and is still revered there today.

teile.einleitung: Sibiu is an old city in Transylvania, a region in the middle of Romania. In German it is called Hermannstadt. The city was founded in the Middle Ages by German-speaking settlers and was European Capital of Culture in 2007.
wichtigste: Sibiu lies in Transylvania in Romania.
In German the city is called Hermannstadt.
It was founded by German-speaking settlers.
In 2007 Sibiu was European Capital of Culture together with Luxembourg.
The old town is known for its houses with “eyes” on the roofs.

abschnitte.titel: A city of the Transylvanian Saxons
abschnitte.text: In the 12th century, Hungarian kings brought settlers from the west to **Transylvania**. They spoke German and were later called **Transylvanian Saxons**. Hermannstadt became their most important place. The city was given strong walls and towers to protect itself. For a long time, people who spoke German, Romanian and Hungarian lived together here. Today the great majority speak Romanian.

The old town has three large squares: the Large Square, the Small Square and the Huet Square. Typical features are roofs with small, narrow dormer windows. They look like half-closed eyes, so people say the houses of Sibiu watch the people. The iron **Bridge of Lies** is also well known, and there are many stories about it. The **Brukenthal Museum** on the Large Square is regarded as the oldest museum in Romania.

In 2007 Romania joined the **European Union**. In the same year Sibiu was **European Capital of Culture**. The city shared the title with **Luxembourg**, because the two are linked by their history: many of the early settlers came from the area around Luxembourg and the Rhineland. For that year the old town was thoroughly renovated. Since then many more visitors have come to the city.

gewusst: The city has three names: Hermannstadt in German, Sibiu in Romanian and Nagyszeben in Hungarian.
The dialect of the Transylvanian Saxons is similar to Luxembourgish, so speakers of the two dialects can partly understand each other.

teile.einleitung: Jože Plečnik was a Slovenian architect. He shaped the city of Ljubljana with bridges, squares, parks and buildings. His works in Ljubljana have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021.
wichtigste: Jože Plečnik was an architect from Slovenia.
He lived from 1872 to 1957.
He shaped Ljubljana with many buildings, such as the Triple Bridge.
He also worked in Vienna and Prague.
His works in Ljubljana have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021.

abschnitte.text: Jože Plečnik was born in **Ljubljana** in **1872** and died there in **1957**. At first he learned the trade of his father, who was a carpenter. Later he studied architecture in **Vienna** and built several buildings there. After that he worked in **Prague**, where he redesigned parts of **Prague Castle**. Back in Ljubljana, in the first half of the 20th century he designed many buildings for his home city.

His best-known work is the **Triple Bridge** in the centre. Plečnik added two narrow footbridges to an old bridge over the River Ljubljanica, one on the left and one on the right. In this way three bridges came to stand side by side. He also designed the riverside paths, the **market halls** by the river and the **National and University Library**. Plečnik mixed forms from antiquity with his own ideas. That is why his buildings are unmistakable.

Plečnik wanted to make Ljubljana a beautiful capital for the Slovenes. He therefore planned not just single buildings, but whole streets, squares and green spaces. Since **2021** his works in Ljubljana have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. UNESCO praises how he designed the city as a whole, with people at the centre.

gewusst: The Slovenian 10 cent coin shows a design by Plečnik for a parliament building that was never built.

teile.einleitung: The mistral is a cold, dry north wind in the south of France. It blows through the Rhône Valley to the Mediterranean and shapes the landscape and the building style of Provence.
wichtigste: The mistral is a cold north wind in the Rhône Valley.
Between the Alps and the Cévennes it is accelerated as if in a nozzle.
It often arises with a high over the Bay of Biscay and a low over the Gulf of Genoa.
It blows most often in winter and spring.
The name means “masterly” in Occitan.
Rows of cypresses protect fields and gardens from the wind.

abschnitte.titel: A wind as if from a nozzle
abschnitte.text: The **mistral** streams from the north through the **Rhône Valley** to the Mediterranean. The valley lies between the foothills of the **Alps** and the **Cévennes** at the edge of the Massif Central. This narrowing accelerates the air as if in a **nozzle**. Typical is a **high** over the Bay of Biscay and a **low** over the Gulf of Genoa. Then cold air flows south, often strengthened by a cold front.

The mistral blows most often and most strongly in **winter** and **spring**, but it can come in any season. It often lasts one to several days. It usually brings a clear, blue sky, but also cold. The name comes from Occitan, an old language of southern France, and means **“masterly”**. It goes back to the Latin word magistralis.

A strong mistral blows from the land out to sea. It pushes the warm **surface water** in the **Gulf of Lion** out onto the open sea. Colder water rises from the depths. That is why the sea on the coast often cools down markedly after a mistral, even in the middle of summer.

The people of Provence have adapted to the wind. The traditional farmhouses, the **mas**, turn their backs to the north wind and open their front to the **south**. The north side usually has only a few small windows. Many church towers have, instead of closed bell chambers, open frames of **wrought iron** through which the wind can blow unhindered. Long rows of **cypresses** slow the wind and protect fields and gardens.

The painter **Vincent van Gogh** lived in Provence in 1888 and 1889, including in **Arles**. He liked to paint outdoors in nature. In his letters he described how the mistral rattled his easel and made painting hard for him. Even so, many of his best-known pictures were made there.

gewusst: The cypresses in Provence often did not grow by chance, but were planted as a windbreak.
In Provence they say the mistral often blows for three, six or nine days.

teile.einleitung: Kosovo is a small country on the Balkan Peninsula in the south-east of Europe. It declared its independence from Serbia in 2008. Many people from Kosovo also live in Switzerland today.
wichtigste: Kosovo declared itself independent on 17 February 2008.
Many states, including Switzerland, have recognised Kosovo, but Serbia has not.
The capital is called Pristina.
Kosovo borders Serbia, Montenegro, Albania and North Macedonia and has no access to the sea.
The official languages are Albanian and Serbian.
People pay with the euro, although Kosovo does not belong to the EU.

abschnitte.text: Kosovo lies in the middle of the **Balkan Peninsula**. It is a **landlocked country**, which means it has no access to the sea. Its neighbouring countries are **Serbia**, **Montenegro**, **Albania** and **North Macedonia**. Inside there are wide plains, and mountains rise at the edge. Bulgaria lies further east and does not border Kosovo.

For a long time Kosovo belonged to Yugoslavia and later to Serbia. At the end of the 1990s a **war** broke out, and at its end in 1999 NATO intervened. After that the **UN** administered the territory, and international troops provided security. On **17 February 2008** Kosovo declared its **independence**. Serbia still regards Kosovo as part of its state territory, so the question remains disputed.

The great majority of the population speak **Albanian**. **Serbian** is also an **official language** across the country, that is, a language in which public authorities work. Smaller groups such as Bosniaks, Turks and Roma also live in the country. Compared with other countries in Europe, the population of Kosovo is very young.

In Kosovo people pay with the **euro**, although the country is not a member of the **European Union**. Kosovo introduced the euro in **2002**. Before that the **Deutsche Mark** was mainly used. Kosovo does not mint euro coins of its own, but uses the coins and notes of the euro countries.

Switzerland was among the first countries to have **recognised** Kosovo. Since 1999 the Swiss Army has taken part in the international peacekeeping force **KFOR** with the **Swisscoy**. In addition, many people with roots in Kosovo live in Switzerland. So the two countries are closely connected.

gewusst: The flag of Kosovo shows the golden outline map of the country and six white stars on a blue background.
Kosovo is one of the youngest states in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Nessebar is an old town on a small peninsula on the Black Sea in Bulgaria. Its old town with many medieval churches is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Nessebar lies on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria.
The old town lies on a small peninsula.
The town is over 3000 years old.
It used to be a Greek colony.
The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Nessebar** is over **3000 years** old. First the **Thracians** lived here, an ancient people of the region. Later **Greeks** founded a **colony** at this spot, that is, a settlement far from home. They called the town Mesembria. After that it belonged to various empires, among them the Byzantine Empire.

Nessebar is famous for its many **medieval churches** of stone and brick. Some are only ruins now, while others are well preserved. In addition there are old **wooden houses** with a ground floor of stone. Because of these buildings the **old town** is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The old town lies on a small **peninsula** in the **Black Sea**. A narrow causeway links it with the mainland and the new town. Nearby lies the large seaside resort of Sunny Beach. In summer very many tourists come to Nessebar.

gewusst: Nessebar is sometimes called the “Pearl of the Black Sea”.

teile.einleitung: The North Sea is a marginal sea of the Atlantic Ocean in north-western Europe. It is known for ebb and flow, the Wadden Sea, many islands and for oil and gas from the sea floor.
wichtigste: The North Sea lies between Great Britain in the west and Norway, Denmark, Germany and the Netherlands in the east.
About every 12 hours the tide comes in, so roughly twice a day.
Off the coast lies the Wadden Sea, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Sheep often graze on the dykes.
In the North Sea live fish such as the plaice and small shrimps, the North Sea shrimps.
On drilling rigs oil and natural gas are extracted.

abschnitte.text: The North Sea is connected to the **Atlantic**. In the west it is bounded by **Great Britain**, and in the east lie **Norway**, **Denmark**, **Germany** and the **Netherlands**. Belgium and France also have a small stretch of coast. The North Sea is quite shallow, in many places only a few dozen metres deep. Countries such as Austria, Hungary or the Czech Republic, on the other hand, have no sea at all.

On the North Sea **low tide** and **high tide** alternate. This movement is called the **tides**. About every 12 hours the water rises again. At low tide a broad strip of sea floor along the coast dries out, the **Wadden Sea**. Worms, mussels and crabs live there, and many migratory birds rest here.

Off the coast of Lower Saxony lie the **East Frisian Islands** such as Borkum, Juist and Norderney. Off Schleswig-Holstein lie the **North Frisian Islands** such as Föhr, Amrum and Sylt. To **Sylt** you travel by train over the **Hindenburgdamm**, on which only trains run, including car trains. High **dykes** protect the land from storm surges. On them **sheep** graze, which keep the grass short and tread the ground firm.

The **plaice** is a flat fish with orange spots. It lies well camouflaged on the sandy bottom. The **North Sea shrimp** is really a small **prawn**. Fishermen catch it with boats called **cutters**, and it is eaten, for example, in a bread roll. On the coasts **seals** also live, which like to rest on sandbanks.

In the North Sea stand large **drilling rigs**. They bring **oil** and **natural gas** up from the sea floor. Norway and Great Britain in particular have become rich from this. Today many **wind farms** are also being built in the North Sea, because strong wind often blows there.

gewusst: The Wadden Sea is the largest continuous area of mudflats in the world.
The Hindenburgdamm to Sylt is about 11 kilometres long and opened in 1927.

teile.einleitung: The Orkney Islands are a group of islands off the north coast of Scotland. They are known for very old Stone Age buildings and their long Norse history.
wichtigste: The Orkney Islands lie north of the Scottish mainland between the Atlantic and the North Sea.
The main town is Kirkwall on the main island, Mainland.
Skara Brae is a Stone Age village about 5000 years old.
Until 1468 the islands belonged to Norway.
Today they belong to Scotland and so to the United Kingdom.

abschnitte.text: The Orkney Islands lie north of the Scottish mainland, where the **Atlantic** and the **North Sea** meet. The group consists of about 70 islands, but only about 20 are inhabited. The largest island is called **Mainland**. There lies the main town **Kirkwall** with **St Magnus Cathedral**. Further north still follow the **Shetland Islands** with the main town of Lerwick.

On Orkney there are especially well-preserved buildings from the **Neolithic**. **Skara Brae** is a village about **5000 years** old. In it you can even see beds and shelves made of stone. A **storm** exposed it in **1850** from under the sand. In addition there are stone circles such as the **Ring of Brodgar**. These sites are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For a long time the islands belonged to **Norway**. Vikings lived here, and many place names therefore come from Nordic languages. In **1468** the islands passed to Scotland as a **pledge**, when the Danish-Norwegian king married his daughter to the Scottish king. The pledge was never redeemed.

Between the islands lies **Scapa Flow**, a large sheltered bay. In both world wars the British fleet lay there. In 1919 the German crews scuttled their own warships here. Today scuba divers dive to the wrecks.

gewusst: Skara Brae is older than the pyramids of Giza.
On Orkney it stays light for a very long time in summer, because the islands lie far to the north.

teile.einleitung: The Port of Hamburg is the largest port in Germany. Ships from all over the world arrive here every day, bringing goods in huge metal boxes. But the port is also a place for outings, festivals and music.
wichtigste: The Port of Hamburg is the largest port in Germany.
It lies on the Elbe, which flows into the North Sea.
Goods are transported in large metal boxes called containers.
Giant cranes lift the containers off the ships.
The Speicherstadt with its red brick buildings is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Elbphilharmonie is a concert hall with a wavy roof.
Every Sunday morning the fish market takes place at the port.

abschnitte.text: The Port of Hamburg does not lie directly on the sea, but on the **Elbe**. The ships sail up the river to Hamburg. When they leave the port, they sail down the Elbe into the **North Sea**. From there they go on to all parts of the world. Because ships keep getting bigger, the Elbe has to be dredged deeper again and again so that they do not run aground.

Most goods today travel in **containers**. These are big metal boxes that all have a standard size. That is why they fit on ships, lorries and trains. Giant **cranes** lift the heavy containers off the ship and set them down on land. In some parts of the port the containers are even moved on by vehicles with no driver. Many goods that are sold in Switzerland come to Europe via large North Sea ports such as Hamburg.

The **Speicherstadt** is an old district with warehouses of red brick. The buildings stand on piles in the water, with canals flowing between them. In the past coffee, tea, spices and carpets were stored here. The goods arrived at the buildings directly by boat. Since 2015 the Speicherstadt, together with the neighbouring Kontorhaus district, has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

At the edge of the port stands the **Elbphilharmonie**, a large concert hall. It was built on top of an old brick warehouse. On top of it sits a glass building whose roof looks like waves. It opened in 2017. From a viewing platform you can look far out over the port and the city.

Every Sunday the **fish market** begins very early in the morning. There is not only fish there, but also fruit, flowers and much more. The sellers shout loudly to advertise their goods. Every year in May, Hamburg celebrates its **port birthday**. Then many ships and visitors come, and there are parades on the water and fireworks.

gewusst: The port birthday recalls a document from the year 1189 that gave Hamburg rights for shipping on the Elbe.
A large container ship can carry many thousands of containers at once.

teile.einleitung: Lapland is a region in the far north of Europe. In winter it is dark for a long time there, and in summer it is light for a long time. For a very long time the Sámi, who keep reindeer, have lived here.
wichtigste: Lapland lies in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
The Sámi are the indigenous people of Lapland.
The Arctic Circle runs right across Lapland.
In summer the midnight sun shines.
In winter there is polar night, and you often see the northern lights.
Winters are very cold and snowy.

abschnitte.text: Lapland lies in the **far north of Europe**. It is not a country of its own, but a region that stretches across the north of **Norway**, **Sweden** and **Finland**. A small part also belongs to **Russia**. Right across Lapland runs the **Arctic Circle**, an imaginary line that goes around the Earth in the far north.

The **Sámi** are the **indigenous people** of Lapland. They have lived here for a very long time. Many of them have kept **reindeer** for centuries. In the past they moved through the land with the herds and lived in tents, the **lavvu**. The Sámi have languages of their own and a culture of their own.

In summer the Sun does not set at all at night in Lapland. This is called the **midnight sun**, because it is light even at midnight. In winter it is the other way round: the Sun stays below the horizon for weeks. This dark time is called **polar night**. The reason is the tilted axis of the Earth.

In winter there is a lot of **snow** in Lapland, and it is often far below zero. On clear, dark nights **northern lights** glow in the sky. They are mostly green, sometimes also red or violet. They occur when particles from the **Sun** hit the Earth's atmosphere. Many people travel to Lapland specially to see them.

gewusst: In the town of Rovaniemi in Finland the Arctic Circle runs through the middle of a village dedicated to Father Christmas.
In summer in Lapland you can read a book at midnight without a lamp.

teile.einleitung: The Carpathians are a large mountain range in east-central and eastern Europe. They stretch in a wide arc through several countries. Many wild animals such as bears, wolves and lynx still live there.
wichtigste: On the map the Carpathians form a great arc and are about 1300 kilometres long.
About half of the range lies in Romania.
Slovakia, Poland and Ukraine, among others, have other shares.
The highest part is the High Tatras with Gerlach Peak, about 2655 metres high.
Very many brown bears live in the Carpathians.
The Danube breaks through the mountains at the Iron Gates.

abschnitte.text: The Carpathians stretch in a great **arc** through eastern Europe and are about 1300 kilometres long. They begin at Bratislava on the Danube and reach as far as Romania. Countries such as **Slovakia**, Poland, Ukraine and **Romania** have a share of them. About half lies in Romania. A part there is called the **Southern Carpathians** or Transylvanian Alps.

The highest part of the Carpathians is the **High Tatras** on the border between Slovakia and Poland. There stands the highest peak, **Gerlach Peak**, at about 2655 metres. That makes the Carpathians clearly lower than the Alps, where many peaks are over 4000 metres high. Many parts of the Carpathians are covered with dense forests.

In the Carpathians there are still large, almost untouched **forests**. Very many **brown bears** live there, mainly in Romania. **Wolves** and **lynx** also occur. Some of the old beech forests are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

The **Danube** breaks through the Carpathians on the border between Serbia and Romania. The narrow gorge between the Southern Carpathians and the Balkan Mountains is called the **Iron Gates**. Here the river has dug a narrow valley through the rock. Today large **hydroelectric power stations** dam the Danube at this point.

The region of **Transylvania** in Romania is surrounded by the Carpathians. The well-known horror story of **Dracula** is set in this area. **Bran Castle** is therefore often called “Dracula's Castle”. The story was invented in the 19th century by the writer Bram Stoker.

gewusst: Transylvania is also called Siebenbürgen in German.
With its Carpathian forests, Romania has the largest population of brown bears in the European Union.

teile.einleitung: The Moldoveanu is the highest mountain in Romania. It rises in the Făgăraș Mountains in the Southern Carpathians and is popular with hikers.
wichtigste: At 2544 metres the Moldoveanu is the highest mountain in Romania.
It lies in the Făgăraș Mountains.
The Făgăraș Mountains belong to the Southern Carpathians.
The Carpathians are a long mountain arc in eastern Europe.
The summit can only be reached on foot.

abschnitte.text: The **Moldoveanu** is **2544 metres** high and so the highest mountain in Romania. It stands in the **Făgăraș Mountains**, a long and steep mountain chain in the middle of the country. Very close by lies the Negoiu, the second highest mountain in Romania. For comparison: many Swiss Alpine peaks are much higher, and the Carpathians are lower than the Alps overall.

The **Carpathians** form a great arc through several countries in eastern Europe. The southern part is called the **Southern Carpathians** or also the Transylvanian Alps. In the forests of the Carpathians bears, wolves and lynx still live. In Romania the range separates the region of Transylvania from the south of the country.

There is no road to the summit, so you have to **hike**. The tours usually take a long time, and hikers often stay overnight in mountain huts. At the top stands a summit marker, and in clear weather you can see far over the mountains. In winter there is a lot of snow there, and then the climb is only for experienced mountaineers.

gewusst: Across the Făgăraș Mountains runs the well-known mountain road Transfăgărășan, one of the most winding roads in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Colosseum is a huge arena in the centre of Rome. The ancient Romans built it almost 2000 years ago. There tens of thousands of people watched fights and games.
wichtigste: The Colosseum is an amphitheatre, an arena with rows of seats all around.
It was built by the ancient Romans and opened in the year AD 80.
Seen from above, it is oval.
About 50,000 spectators had room inside it.
Gladiators fought there in front of an audience.
Beneath the floor of the arena there were passages and rooms.

abschnitte.text: The Colosseum is an **amphitheatre**, that is, an arena with rows of seats all around. Emperor **Vespasian** had building begin, and it was opened in the year **AD 80** under his son Titus. That is almost 2000 years ago. It was the largest arena in the whole **Roman Empire**. It was built mainly of stone, bricks and a kind of Roman concrete.

Great **games** took place in the Colosseum. **Gladiators** were fighters who took on each other in the arena to entertain the audience. Often they were slaves or prisoners of war who were trained for it. There were also shows with wild animals from distant lands. Admission was mostly free for the spectators.

Seen from above, the Colosseum has the shape of an **oval**, that is, rounded and elongated. That way all the spectators could see into the arena well. About **50,000** people had room, roughly as many as in a large football stadium. More than 80 entrances meant that the building could be filled and emptied quickly. When it was sunny, a large awning could be stretched over the seating.

Under the wooden floor of the arena lay many **passages** and **chambers**. There fighters and animals waited for their turn to appear. With lifts and trapdoors they could suddenly appear in the arena. This part is called the **hypogeum**. Today the floor is missing in many places, so you can see the passages from above.

Over the centuries the Colosseum was damaged by **earthquakes**. Many stones were carried off for other buildings in Rome. Even so, a large part is still standing. Today the Colosseum is a landmark of Rome and, together with the old town, a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Millions of people visit it every year.

gewusst: The name Colosseum probably comes from a huge statue, the Colossus of Nero, which stood nearby.
The Colosseum is shown on the Italian 5 cent coin.

teile.einleitung: The beluga is a giant fish from the sturgeon family. It lives in the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea and swims far up the rivers to spawn, for example into the Danube. Today it is severely threatened.
wichtigste: The beluga is a species of sturgeon.
It can grow to several metres in length.
It is a migratory fish and travels from the sea into the rivers.
Its eggs are highly sought after as caviar.
The beluga is now threatened with extinction.

abschnitte.text: The beluga belongs to the **sturgeons**, a very old group of fish. Instead of scales, it has rows of bony plates on its back and sides. It can grow to several metres in length and is therefore one of the largest freshwater fish in the world. Belugas can live to a great age, some of them over a hundred years. In German it is called **Hausen**.

abschnitte.titel: From the sea into the Danube
abschnitte.text: The beluga spends most of its time in the **Black Sea** or the **Caspian Sea**. To spawn, it swims up the rivers, for example through the Danube Delta into the **Danube**. Fish that migrate between sea and river like this are called **migratory fish**. In the past belugas travelled far upstream in the Danube. Today large **dams**, such as the one at the Iron Gates between Serbia and Romania, block the way.

The eggs of the beluga are sold as **beluga caviar** and are very expensive. That is why the fish was caught heavily for a long time, often illegally too. Together with the dams, this has meant that the beluga is now **threatened with extinction**. Trade is strictly regulated, and in several countries there are programmes to breed young sturgeons and release them into the rivers.

gewusst: Sturgeons already existed in the time of the dinosaurs, and they are regarded as living fossils.
