**Vienna** is the capital and the largest city of the country. It is famous for music, palaces and coffee houses. Famous composers such as **Mozart** came from Austria, and he was born in Salzburg. Since 1995 Austria has been a member of the **European Union** and pays with the euro.

Switzerland and Austria border each other in the east of Switzerland, for example in the Lower Engadine and on the **Rhine** near St Gallen. Like Switzerland, Austria is a **neutral** country. In both countries people speak German, but with their own words and dialects.

gewusst: The Inn, an important river of Austria, rises in Switzerland.
In Austria people often say “Jänner” for January.

teile.einleitung: Neum is a small town in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here the country has its only short access to the sea, the Adriatic.
wichtigste: Neum lies on the Adriatic.
At Neum Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches the sea along about 20 kilometres.
It is the country's only access to the sea.
The coastal strip separates the area around Dubrovnik from the rest of Croatia.
Neum is a seaside resort.

abschnitte.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina lies almost entirely inland. Only at **Neum** does the country reach the **sea**, along about **20 kilometres** of coast. This narrow strip lies between Croatian territory. It separates the area around **Dubrovnik** from the rest of **Croatia**.

Anyone who used to drive from Split to Dubrovnik had to go through Neum and so cross a border twice. Croatia therefore built a large **bridge** to the **Pelješac** peninsula. It opened in **2022**. Since then you can drive to Dubrovnik on Croatian territory without having to pass through Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Neum is a small **seaside resort** with hotels and beaches. Many visitors come from Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, because it is the country's only coast. The houses stand on a slope above the sea. In front of the town lies a sheltered bay.

gewusst: The border at Neum goes back to a very old border of the Republic of Ragusa, the former city state of Dubrovnik.

teile.einleitung: Ireland has a mild, damp maritime climate. Winters are seldom really cold and summers seldom really hot. The reason is the Atlantic and the westerly winds, which bring a lot of rain.
wichtigste: According to Köppen, the whole of Ireland has the climate Cfb: temperate, damp all year round, with mild summers.
The rain-bearing winds mostly come from the west, from the Atlantic.
Valentia Island in the west gets almost twice as much rain as Dublin.
Dublin lies in the lee of the westerly winds and mountains and is therefore drier.
In the west, blanket bogs cover large areas.
The cold record of minus 19.1 degrees dates from 1881, and the heat record of 33.3 degrees from 1887.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Köppen** classification, the whole of Ireland has the climate **Cfb**. This means: temperate, damp all year round, with warm but not hot summers. It is the typical **oceanic climate** of western Europe. The sea evens out the temperatures, warming in winter and cooling in summer. A comparison shows how strong the effect is: **Happy Valley-Goose Bay** in Canada lies at almost the same latitude as Dublin, but has a January average far below minus 10 degrees.

Most rain clouds arrive with the **westerly winds** from the Atlantic. They rain out first on the west coast and on the mountains. On **Valentia Island** about 1400 millimetres of rain fall a year, and in **Dublin** only about 714 millimetres. Dublin lies in the **lee**, that is, on the side away from the wind. By the time the air reaches the east coast, it has already lost a lot of moisture.

Because of the heavy rainfall, **blanket bogs** cover large areas in the west. It rains so often there that **peat** lies over the land like a blanket. In Kerry and West Cork the **fuchsia**, which originally comes from South America, grows wild in long hedges. It thrives in the mild, almost frost-free winters and lines many roads with red flowers.

On 16 January 1881 the temperature at **Markree Castle** in County Sligo fell to **minus 19.1 degrees**. This is the cold record for Ireland. The heat record is held by **Kilkenny Castle** with 33.3 degrees on 26 June 1887, although the accuracy of this old measurement is doubted. Values like these are extremely rare in Ireland because of the sea.

In autumn and winter, powerful **storm lows** often move across Ireland. In October 2017 the former hurricane **Ophelia** hit the island. It had become a strong hurricane unusually far to the east in the Atlantic. On 16 October 2017 it brought severe gusts of storm force and claimed lives.

gewusst: Because of the lots of rain and green meadows, Ireland is often called “the Emerald Isle”.
Ophelia is regarded as the easternmost major hurricane in the Atlantic since reliable records began.

teile.einleitung: The Kalevala is the national epic of Finland. An epic is a long story in verse about heroes and adventures. The Kalevala has had a strong influence on the national feeling of the Finns.
wichtigste: The Kalevala was put together in the 19th century by Elias Lönnrot.
It is based on old Finnish and Karelian folk songs.
The first edition appeared in 1835, and an extended version in 1849.
An important figure is the wise singer Väinämöinen.
The work strengthened the national feeling of the Finns.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century the doctor **Elias Lönnrot** travelled through Finland and above all through **Karelia**. There many people still sang old songs that had never been written down. Lönnrot wrote them down and joined them together into one great story. The first edition appeared in 1835, and a longer version in 1849.

The Kalevala tells of the creation of the world and of heroes with magical powers. The most important figure is the old, wise singer **Väinämöinen**, who can work magic with his singing. A smith called Ilmarinen forges the **Sampo**, a mysterious object that brings luck and prosperity. A great quarrel arises over it.

At that time Finland belonged to the Russian Empire, and before that for a long time to Sweden. The Kalevala showed that the Finns have their own old culture and language. That is why it strongly strengthened **national feeling**. Many artists were inspired by it, such as the composer **Jean Sibelius**. On 28 February Finland celebrates Kalevala Day.

gewusst: The writer J. R. R. Tolkien knew the Kalevala and was inspired by it for his invented worlds.

teile.einleitung: In the night of 26 April 1986 a reactor exploded at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant. It was the worst accident in the history of civil nuclear energy, and radioactive substances spread over the whole of Europe.
wichtigste: The disaster happened on 26 April 1986 in Unit 4 of the plant in what is now Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union.
During a safety test, operating errors and design flaws led to the explosion.
The reactor was of the RBMK type.
The nearby town of Pripyat was evacuated on 27 April.
An exclusion zone of about 30 kilometres arose around the plant.
Chernobyl was rated at the highest INES level, 7.
In Switzerland, Ticino was the most affected.

abschnitte.text: In Unit 4 a **safety test** was carried out. They wanted to check whether the turbines, as they ran down, could still supply enough electricity for the cooling pumps. The reactor was of the **RBMK** type, a Soviet design with graphite. It had **design weaknesses** that could lead to a dangerous rise in power at low output. Together with **operating errors** this led to the explosion and a fire.

The town of **Pripyat**, in which the power plant workers lived, was evacuated on **27 April 1986**. About 49,000 people had to leave it. It is still a ghost town today. Later an **exclusion zone** with a radius of about **30 kilometres** was set up. Over 100,000 people lost their homes.

The Soviet Union at first kept silent about the disaster. On **28 April** measuring instruments at the Swedish nuclear power plant **Forsmark** set off alarms. This is how the world found out. In **Switzerland** **Ticino** was the most affected, because at the beginning of May heavy rain washed radioactive particles out of the air. There, for example, fishing bans were imposed on **Lake Lugano**.

Some of the substances decay quickly: **iodine-131**, for example, is half gone after about 8 days. **Caesium-137**, on the other hand, has a **half-life** of about **30 years**. That means that after 30 years only half has decayed. That is why mushrooms and wild boar are still contaminated in some areas today.

As early as 1986 a concrete shell was built over the reactor, the **sarcophagus**. Over time it became brittle. That is why a huge arched hall was built next to it, the **New Safe Confinement**. In November **2016** it was slid over the reactor. It is meant to last about 100 years.

gewusst: Apart from Chernobyl, only the Fukushima accident of 2011 was rated at the highest INES level, 7.
The New Safe Confinement is one of the largest movable structures ever built.

teile.einleitung: The Oder is a large river in central Europe. It flows from the Czech Republic through Poland to the Baltic Sea and forms a long stretch of the border between Germany and Poland.
wichtigste: The Oder is about 860 kilometres long.
It rises in the Oder Mountains in the Czech Republic.
Most of the river lies in Poland.
Together with the Neisse it forms the border between Germany and Poland.
In Polish and Czech it is called “Odra”.
It flows into the Baltic Sea by way of the Szczecin Lagoon.

abschnitte.text: The Oder begins in the **Oder Mountains** in the **Czech Republic**. After that it flows north through **Poland**. It is about **860 kilometres** long. Shortly before the sea it reaches the **Szczecin Lagoon**, a large lagoon. From there the water reaches the **Baltic Sea**. In Polish and Czech the river is called **Odra**.

A long stretch of the Oder separates **Germany** and **Poland**. Together with the **Neisse** it forms the **Oder-Neisse line**. This border was fixed in 1945 after the Second World War. Today both countries belong to the EU, and you can simply drive across on bridges.

The large Polish city of **Breslau**, in Polish **Wrocław**, lies on the Oder. It has many islands and bridges. On the border lies **Frankfurt (Oder)**. It has the same name as Frankfurt am Main, but is a different city. Opposite lies the Polish town of Słubice. Near the mouth lies the port city of **Stettin**, in Polish Szczecin.

In the valley of the Oder there are large **floodplains**, meadows and woods that are flooded in high water. Many birds such as storks and cranes live there. In **1997** there was a severe **Oder flood** that caused great damage in the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany. Afterwards many dykes were strengthened.

gewusst: The Oder and the Neisse together form one of the most important borders in Europe.
In Frankfurt (Oder) and Słubice there is a university where students from both countries study.

teile.einleitung: Norway is an elongated country in the north of Europe with a very long coast, deep fjords and high mountains. Like Switzerland, it does not belong to the European Union.
wichtigste: The capital of Norway is Oslo.
People pay with the Norwegian krone.
The flag is red with a blue cross with a white border.
The national holiday is 17 May, the day of the constitution of 1814.
Until 1905 Norway was joined in a union with Sweden.
Oil and natural gas from the North Sea make Norway rich.
Like Switzerland, Norway is a member of EFTA.

abschnitte.text: Norway lies in the west of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In the west it borders the **North Sea** and the **North Atlantic**. The coast is very long, because deep arms of the sea reach far inland. These are called **fjords**. They formed when **glaciers** scoured out valleys in the ice age. Right in the north lies the **North Cape**, a cliff over 300 metres high.

On **17 May 1814** Norway got its **constitution**. That is why on this day many children march in parades through the streets. After that Norway was joined until **1905** in a **union with Sweden**, with a shared king. In 1905 Norway became fully independent. Today it is a **monarchy** with a king and an elected parliament.

In Norway people pay with the **Norwegian krone**. The country is not a member of the **EU**, and in two votes the people said No. Like Switzerland, however, Norway belongs to **EFTA**, the European Free Trade Association. Iceland and Liechtenstein also belong to it.

Since the **1970s** Norway has extracted large amounts of **oil** and **natural gas** from the North Sea. The state invests part of the revenue in a huge **fund**. **Fishing**, for example salmon farming, and electricity from **hydropower** are also important.

On the west coast lies **Bergen**. The harbour district of **Bryggen** with its old colourful wooden houses is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In Norwegian fairy tales **trolls** live in mountains and forests. In Norway you often see them as figures in souvenir shops.

gewusst: In the north of Norway the Sun does not set for weeks in summer. This is called the midnight sun.
The Norwegian Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911.

teile.einleitung: Hamburg lies in the north of Germany on the Elbe and is the second largest city in the country after Berlin. The city is known for its huge port, its many bridges and canals, and its long history as a trading city.
wichtigste: Hamburg is the second largest city in Germany.
Hamburg is also a federal state in its own right, a so-called city state.
The Port of Hamburg is the largest seaport in Germany.
The Alster is dammed to form two lakes in the middle of the city.
Hamburg belonged to the Hanseatic League and is officially called the “Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg”.
The Old Elbe Tunnel of 1911 leads under the Elbe for pedestrians.
The largest model railway in the world is in the Miniatur Wunderland.

abschnitte.text: Hamburg has about 1.9 million inhabitants (as of around 2023) and is therefore the second largest city in Germany after Berlin. Hamburg is also a **federal state** in its own right. This kind of state is called a **city state**, like Berlin and Bremen. In Switzerland there is something similar in the canton of Basel-Stadt, which consists almost only of the city of Basel. The magnificent **town hall** in the city centre is the seat of the government and parliament.

Hamburg lies on the **Elbe**, about 100 kilometres from the open sea. Even so, the Port of Hamburg is the largest seaport in Germany and one of the largest container ports in Europe. Even in the Middle Ages Hamburg was an important trading city. It belonged to the **Hanseatic League**, an alliance of merchants and towns on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. That is why the city is still officially called the “Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg”.

abschnitte.titel: Water in the middle of the city
abschnitte.text: In the middle of Hamburg, the river **Alster** is dammed to form two lakes: the smaller **Binnenalster** and the larger **Aussenalster**. People sail, row and paddle on the Aussenalster. There are also many canals, called **fleets**. Hamburg has a great many bridges, more than Venice and Amsterdam put together. That is why water plays a big part in the everyday life of the city.

The **Old Elbe Tunnel** was opened in 1911. It links the Landungsbrücken in the district of St Pauli with the other side of the Elbe. Pedestrians and cyclists go down in large lifts and then walk through two tiled tubes. In the past it was used mainly by dock workers on their way to work. Today it is also very popular with tourists.

In the **Speicherstadt**, an old district with warehouses of red brick, lies the **Miniatur Wunderland**. It shows the largest model railway in the world, with thousands of metres of track, cities in miniature and even an airport. It is one of the most visited sights in Hamburg. Other landmarks are the church of **St Michael's**, which people call “Michel”, and the concert hall **Elbphilharmonie**.

gewusst: Hamburg has more bridges than Venice and Amsterdam put together.
The Speicherstadt has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.
The Miniatur Wunderland also has a miniature Switzerland with mountains and mountain railways.

teile.einleitung: Herzegovina is the southern part of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its name means “land of the duke” and goes back to a ruler of the 15th century. The most important city is Mostar with its famous bridge.
wichtigste: Herzegovina is the south of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The name comes from the noble title “duke”.
In the 15th century the ruler of the region called himself duke.
The largest city is Mostar on the River Neretva.
The Old Bridge of Mostar is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In the 15th century the area was ruled by a prince called **Stjepan Vukčić Kosača**. He called himself “**duke**”, a title that had been taken over from German. In the local language this became “herceg”. The area was then called the land of the duke, so “**Herzegovina**”, which means roughly “land of the duke”. Shortly afterwards the Ottoman Empire conquered the region.

The largest city in Herzegovina is **Mostar** on the River **Neretva**. Its landmark is the **Old Bridge**, a stone arch from the 16th century. It was destroyed in the war in 1993 and then rebuilt using old techniques. Since 2005 the old town with the bridge has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. In summer, brave men jump from the bridge into the river, an old tradition.

Herzegovina lies close to the Adriatic, but has only a very short access to the sea. A large part of the country consists of barren **karst**, a limestone rock with caves and little water on the surface. The climate in the south is warm and dry, almost like the Mediterranean. That is why wine, figs and pomegranates are grown here. The waterfalls of **Kravica** are also well known.

gewusst: Bosnia and Herzegovina has only a very short stretch of coast on the Adriatic, around the town of Neum.
The Neretva is known for its very clear, green-blue water.

teile.einleitung: Jotunheimen is a mountain massif in the south of Norway. The highest mountains in the country and in the whole of northern Europe lie here. The name means “home of the giants”.
wichtigste: Jotunheimen is a mountain range in southern Norway.
The highest mountains in Norway lie there.
The name means “home of the giants”.
There are over 250 peaks higher than 1900 metres.
The highest mountain is Galdhøpiggen at about 2469 metres.

abschnitte.text: The name **Jotunheimen** comes from the world of Norse legend. There the **jotnar** were mighty giants, and Jotunheim was their home. That suits the wild, rugged mountains. In Jotunheimen there are over **250 peaks** higher than 1900 metres. Between them lie glaciers, deep valleys and many lakes.

The highest mountain is **Galdhøpiggen** at about 2469 metres. It is the highest mountain in Norway and in the whole of northern Europe. Just behind it comes **Glittertind**. Compared with the Swiss Alps, these mountains are lower. But because Norway lies so far north, there are already large glaciers and a lot of snow at this height.

A large part of the mountains has been protected as a **national park** since 1980. Jotunheimen is one of the most popular hiking areas in Norway. There is a dense network of paths and **mountain huts**. The hike over the ridge **Besseggen** is especially well known. On one side lies a dark blue lake, and on the other a greenish one that lies much lower.

gewusst: In summer Galdhøpiggen can be climbed with a mountain guide over a glacier, but there is also a path without a glacier.

teile.einleitung: Loch Ness is a long, deep lake in the north of Scotland. It is world famous because of Nessie, a lake monster from legends and stories that has never been proved to exist.
wichtigste: The Scottish word “loch” means lake.
Loch Ness lies in the north of Scotland.
At its deepest point the lake is about 230 metres deep.
It holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales put together.
Peat from the ground colours the water dark brown.
On the shore stands the ruined castle of Urquhart Castle.
The monster Nessie has never been proved to exist.

abschnitte.text: Loch Ness lies in a long valley that runs right across the Scottish Highlands. The lake is about 37 kilometres long, but only a few kilometres wide. At the northern end the water flows over the River Ness to the town of **Inverness** and into the sea. The word **loch** is Scottish and simply means lake.

At its deepest point Loch Ness measures about **230 metres**. Because it is so deep, it holds huge amounts of fresh water, more than all the lakes of England and Wales together. Streams bring fine particles of **peat** into the lake. Peat is a soil made of old, not fully rotted plants. It colours the water dark brown, so after only a few metres you can hardly see anything.

For a long time people have told of a large animal in the lake. The monster **Nessie** became famous in the 1930s, when newspapers printed reports and photographs. One especially well-known photograph later turned out to be a fake. Researchers have examined the lake with sonar and other equipment, but have never found a monster. Nessie remains a legend that attracts many visitors.

Right on the shore stands the ruin of **Urquhart Castle**, an old castle on a headland. Over the centuries it was fought over several times and in the end destroyed. Today it is one of the most popular destinations for trips in Scotland. From the walls you look far out over the lake, and some visitors keep a lookout for Nessie.

Loch Ness is part of the **Caledonian Canal**, a waterway right across Scotland. It links several lakes with canals and locks. This means boats can travel from the east coast to the west coast without sailing around the north of Scotland. Today mainly pleasure cruisers and leisure boats travel there.

gewusst: Loch Ness is so deep that even very tall buildings would disappear in it.
Because of the great mass of water, Loch Ness practically never freezes over, even in cold winters.

teile.einleitung: The Palace of Westminster is the building in London in which the British Parliament meets. It stands on the Thames and, with its clock tower, is one of the best-known buildings in the world.
wichtigste: In the Palace of Westminster the House of Commons and the House of Lords meet.
The palace stands in London on the bank of the Thames.
After a great fire in 1834 it was rebuilt.
The famous bell Big Ben hangs in the clock tower of the palace.
The palace is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The British Parliament has two chambers. In the **House of Commons** sit the elected members. In the **House of Lords** sit members who are not elected by the people. Both meet in the **Palace of Westminster**. In Switzerland too, parliament has two chambers, the National Council and the Council of States, in the **Federal Palace** in Bern.

In the Middle Ages a royal palace already stood on this spot. In **1834** a great **fire** destroyed most of it. Afterwards the palace was rebuilt to plans by the architect **Charles Barry**, and Augustus Pugin designed many of the decorations. The style is called **Gothic Revival**, and it imitates churches of the Middle Ages. The old **Westminster Hall** survived and is the oldest part.

At the northern end stands the tall **clock tower**. Since 2012 it has been called the **Elizabeth Tower**. Many people call it Big Ben, but **Big Ben** is really the name of the great **bell** in the tower. Its chime is very well known in Britain and, for example, rings in the new year on the radio.

Together with the nearby **Westminster Abbey**, a large church, the palace is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. It has over a thousand rooms and long corridors. The palace is old and will need extensive renovation in the coming years.

gewusst: The Palace of Westminster is still officially a royal palace.
Westminster Hall is over 900 years old.

teile.einleitung: The North Atlantic Current is a warm ocean current that continues the Gulf Stream to the north-east. It brings warmth to Europe and divides into several branches reaching as far as the Arctic.
wichtigste: The North Atlantic Current continues the Gulf Stream towards Europe.
Off Norway it flows on as the Norwegian Current.
The North Cape Current and the West Spitsbergen Current bring warm water into the Arctic.
The Irminger Current flows past Iceland to the south and west.
To the south the Canary Current branches off.
In the far north the water sinks and forms North Atlantic Deep Water.

abschnitte.text: The **Gulf Stream** brings warm water from the area of the Gulf of Mexico to the north. Off North America it turns east and becomes the **North Atlantic Current**. This flows across the Atlantic towards Europe. It ensures that it is milder in western and northern Europe than in other places at the same latitude. Where the warm current meets the cold **Labrador Current** off **Newfoundland**, damp air cools down and there is very often **fog**.

Off Scandinavia the water flows on as the **Norwegian Current**. Around northern Norway the **North Cape Current** reaches the **Barents Sea**, whose south-west therefore stays largely ice-free in winter. The northernmost branch is the **West Spitsbergen Current**. It keeps the west coast of **Svalbard** free of ice for longer than the east coast. The **Irminger Current** branches off to the west and flows around **Iceland** in the south and west.

Not all the water flows north. Part of it turns south off Europe and flows as the relatively cool **Canary Current** along Portugal and north-west Africa. This closes a great circle of currents, the **subtropical gyre** of the North Atlantic. Such circles exist in all the large oceans.

In the **Nordic Seas** and in the **Labrador Sea** the salty water cools strongly. Cold, salty water is **denser** and so heavier, which is why it sinks into the depths. This is how **North Atlantic Deep Water** forms, which flows south far below. This whole system is called the **Atlantic meridional overturning circulation**.

How mild the current makes things can be seen in the north-west of Scotland. There **Osgood Mackenzie** laid out the **Inverewe Garden** in 1862. Thanks to almost frost-free winters, plants from all over the world grow there, at almost **58 degrees north**. South of Greenland, on the other hand, lies the **“Cold Blob”**, where the sea has hardly warmed or has even cooled. Many researchers see in it a possible sign that the overturning circulation is weakening.

gewusst: Without the North Atlantic Current the winters in Norway and Great Britain would be much colder.
The North Cape Current brings so much warmth that the port of Murmansk in Russia stays ice-free despite lying north of the Arctic Circle.

teile.einleitung: Mont-Saint-Michel is a small rock off the coast of France with an old monastery perched on it. Depending on the tides it lies in the sea or in the mudflats, and it is among the best-known sights in France.
wichtigste: Mont-Saint-Michel is a rock with a monastery in a bay of the sea.
It lies in Normandy, near the border with Brittany.
On the tip of the spire stands a golden figure of the Archangel Michael.
Monks lived in the monastery for many centuries.
Since 2014 a long bridge has led from the mainland to the rock.
Since 1979 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Mont-Saint-Michel** is a small granite rock in a wide bay in the north of France. It lies in **Normandy**, very close to the border with **Brittany**. In the bay there are very strong **tides**: at low tide the sea draws back far, and at high tide it quickly returns. That is why the mountain sometimes looks like an island and sometimes like a hill in the sand.

At the very top stands an old **monastery** with a church. For many centuries **monks** lived there, who prayed and kept extending the buildings. This is how a huge building of stone arose that looks like part of the rock. On the tip of the church spire stands a golden figure of the **Archangel Michael**. The whole mountain is named after him.

Below the monastery lies a small **village** with a steep, narrow main lane. There are old houses, shops and restaurants. One restaurant has long been famous for its large, fluffy **omelette**. For it the eggs are whisked for a long time and cooked over the fire.

abschnitte.titel: The bridge and the World Heritage
abschnitte.text: In the past a causeway led to the rock, but since **2014** there has been a long **bridge**. This means you can cross dry-shod even at high tide, and the water can flow freely under the bridge. Since **1979** Mont-Saint-Michel and its bay have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Every year very many people from all over the world visit it.

gewusst: In the bay of Mont-Saint-Michel the difference between low and high tide is among the largest in Europe.
Anyone who walks across the mudflats at low tide without a guide can be caught out by the quickly rising tide.

teile.einleitung: Lake Ladoga in north-west Russia is the largest lake in Europe. It lies close to Saint Petersburg and is connected to the Baltic Sea. It has played an important role in history, for example in the Second World War.
wichtigste: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe, at about 17,900 square kilometres.
At its deepest point it is about 230 metres deep.
The Svir brings water from Lake Onega, and the Neva flows out to the Baltic Sea.
The northern shore belonged to Finland until 1940.
The “Road of Life” led over the ice to Leningrad.
The Ladoga ringed seal lives in the lake.

abschnitte.text: Lake Ladoga is the **largest lake in Europe**. Depending on the source, it covers about **17,700 to 17,900 square kilometres**. That is over 40 per cent of the area of Switzerland. In the rocky north-west it is about **230 metres** deep, while the south is much shallower. There are numerous islands in the lake, and in winter it mostly freezes over.

The largest inflow by volume is the **Svir**, which comes from **Lake Onega**. From **Lake Ilmen** the **Volkhov** flows into Lake Ladoga. On it lie old towns such as Veliky Novgorod and Staraya Ladoga. The outflow is the **Neva**, which flows to the Baltic Sea at Saint Petersburg. At the outflow stands the fortress of **Shlisselburg**, which Peter the Great captured from the Swedes in **1702**.

In the Second World War the city of **Leningrad**, today's Saint Petersburg, was besieged from **1941 to 1944**. The only link ran across Lake Ladoga. In winter lorries drove over the **ice**, and in summer ships sailed. This route was called the **Road of Life**, because it brought food into the city and people out.

On the island of **Valaam** in the north of the lake stands a famous **Russian Orthodox monastery**. The northern shore of the lake belonged to **Finland** until 1940. In the **Winter War** of 1940 the monks were taken to Finland. After the war the area went to the Soviet Union and today lies in Russia.

A subspecies of the **ringed seal** of its own lives in Lake Ladoga. It occurs only here, which is called **endemic**. The seals are a remnant from the time after the ice age, when the lake was still connected to the sea. Today the **Ladoga ringed seal** is endangered and protected.

gewusst: Seals live in Lake Ladoga, although it is a freshwater lake.
The lake is more than 40 per cent as large as the whole of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: “Overtourism” means that so many visitors come to a place that the life of the locals and also the experience of the visitors suffer. It is a debated topic in many popular travel destinations.
wichtigste: Overtourism describes tourism that excessively harms quality of life and the visitor experience.
The term spread from around 2016.
Barcelona is a well-known example, and its boom began after the 1992 Olympic Games.
When flats become holiday lets, this is called touristification.
Barcelona charges a tourist tax per overnight stay.
Venice charges day visitors an entry fee on some days.

abschnitte.text: Tourism brings **jobs** and money. But when too many visitors come, streets, buses and sights become **overloaded**. **Rents** rise, and locals can hardly find flats any more. This is then called **overtourism**. The term spread from around **2016**. Opinions differ: some want to limit visitors, while others stress how important tourism is for the economy.

For the **1992 Summer Olympics**, Barcelona's beaches, harbour and transport network were rebuilt. Afterwards the number of visitors rose sharply. Under mayor **Ada Colau**, who governed from 2015 to 2023, there was a halt on new hotels in the centre. Her successor **Jaume Collboni** announced in June 2024 that the licences for about 10,000 holiday flats would be allowed to expire by **2028**.

When flats are turned into **holiday lets**, residents move away. Shops for everyday needs are replaced by souvenir shops. This process is called **touristification**. In Barcelona it affects especially the old town and the **Barceloneta** district. In July 2024 thousands protested against rising rents and squirted visitors with **water pistols**.

**Park Güell** in Barcelona, designed by **Antoni Gaudí**, was overcrowded. Since **2013** a ticket has been needed for the monumental zone, and only a limited number of people may enter per hour. Anyone staying overnight in Barcelona pays a **tourist tax** per person and night. **Venice** charges day visitors an **entry fee** on some days.

In Switzerland too there are places with very many visitors, for example **Lucerne** or **Lauterbrunnen**. There people discuss how to steer coaches, traffic and visitor flows better. The aim is for tourism to remain pleasant for the locals and the visitors.

gewusst: Barcelona is among the most visited cities in Europe.
Park Güell was originally planned as a housing estate.

teile.einleitung: Koper is a port town on the short Adriatic coast of Slovenia. Its port is the most important and the only large commercial port in the country. The old town still shows the influence of the former Republic of Venice.
wichtigste: Koper lies on the Adriatic coast of Slovenia.
Slovenia has only about 47 kilometres of sea coast.
Koper is the only large commercial port in the country.
In Italian the town is called Capodistria.
The old town was long shaped by Venice.

abschnitte.text: **Slovenia** has only about 47 kilometres of coast on the **Adriatic**. Koper lies on this short coast, close to the border with Italy and not far from Trieste. The **Port of Koper** is the only large commercial port in the country. Containers, cars and other goods are handled here, including for countries without a sea of their own such as Austria and Hungary.

Koper used to be an island and is now joined to the mainland. For centuries the town belonged to the **Republic of Venice**. You can still see this in the old town with its narrow lanes and the Praetorian Palace on the main square. In the region, **Italian** is spoken as well as Slovenian, which is why the town has the second name **Capodistria**.

gewusst: Koper is bilingual: place signs and street names are written in Slovenian and Italian.

teile.einleitung: The Kornati are a group of many small islands off the coast of Croatia. A large part of them is protected as a national park.
wichtigste: The Kornati lie off the Dalmatian coast in Croatia.
They consist of many barren, mostly uninhabited islands.
A large part is protected as a national park.
The largest island is called Kornat.
The Kornati are very popular with sailors and divers.

abschnitte.text: The **Kornati** are a group of islands in the **Adriatic** off the coast of **Dalmatia** in Croatia. They consist of many islands, islets and rocks. The largest island is called **Kornat** and gave its name to the whole group. Most of the islands are **uninhabited**, and only in summer do some owners come to their small houses.

The islands are **barren**: there are hardly any trees, but a lot of pale limestone and dry-stone walls. In some places high **cliffs** fall steeply into the sea. In the past the inhabitants of the neighbouring islands kept sheep here and grew olives. The water all around is very clear.

A large part of the Kornati has been a **national park** since **1980**. This is meant to protect the landscape and the life in the sea. The islands are especially popular with **sailors** and **divers**. Anyone who goes into the park by boat needs an entry ticket.

gewusst: The Kornati are among the areas richest in islands in the whole Mediterranean.

teile.einleitung: The kuna was the currency of Croatia. In Croatian its name means “marten”. Since 2023 people in Croatia have paid with the euro.
wichtigste: The kuna was the money of Croatia from 1994 to the end of 2022.
“Kuna” is the Croatian word for marten.
In the past, marten pelts were used as a means of payment.
One kuna consisted of 100 lipa.
On 1 January 2023 the kuna was replaced by the euro.

abschnitte.text: The word **kuna** means **marten** in Croatian. The marten is a small predator with soft, valuable fur. In the Middle Ages **marten pelts** were used in the region as a **means of payment**, that is, like money. The name of the currency recalls this. That is why a marten was also shown on kuna coins.

Croatia introduced the kuna in **1994**, a few years after its independence. One kuna was divided into **100 lipa**, just as a franc is divided into 100 centimes. **Lipa** means **linden tree** in Croatian. The kuna was the country's money for almost three decades.

On **1 January 2023** Croatia introduced the **euro**. For one euro you got about 7.5 kuna. The marten has not quite disappeared, though: it can still be seen on the Croatian **1 euro coin**. So the memory of the old currency lives on.

gewusst: The Croatian 1 euro coin also shows a marten, as a reminder of the kuna.
The small unit lipa is named after the linden tree.

teile.einleitung: Krka National Park lies in Croatia near the town of Šibenik. It is famous for the waterfalls of the River Krka, which flow over steps of tufa.
wichtigste: Krka National Park lies near Šibenik in Croatia.
The River Krka forms several waterfalls.
The steps of the waterfalls consist of tufa.
The best-known waterfall is called Skradinski buk.
On a small island in the river stands Visovac Monastery.

abschnitte.text: The **Krka** river flows through a gorge to the sea. On its way it forms several **waterfalls**. Their steps consist of **tufa**: lime from the water is deposited together with mosses and algae and turns to stone. This is how the steps slowly keep growing. The best-known waterfall is called **Skradinski buk** and has many pools and cascades.

The area around the river has been a **national park** since **1985**. It lies near the town of **Šibenik** on the Dalmatian coast. Wooden walkways lead close past the waterfalls. In the park live many birds, fish and bats.

In the middle of the river lies the small island of **Visovac**. On it stands a **monastery** in which Franciscan monks live. Visitors can go there by boat. The island with its trees is one of the prettiest subjects for photographs in the park.

gewusst: On the River Krka stood one of the first hydroelectric power stations for alternating current, which supplied electricity to Šibenik from 1895.

teile.einleitung: Croatia is a country in the south-east of Europe with a long coast on the Adriatic. It is known for its islands, old towns and national parks. Since 2013 Croatia has belonged to the European Union.
wichtigste: Croatia lies on the Adriatic, a part of the Mediterranean.
The capital is Zagreb.
On 25 June 1991 Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia.
On 1 July 2013 Croatia became the 28th member of the EU.
Since 1 January 2023 people pay with the euro instead of the kuna.
In Split stands the palace of the Roman emperor Diocletian.

abschnitte.text: Croatia has a very long coast on the **Adriatic**. The Adriatic is a part of the **Mediterranean**. Off the coast lie more than a thousand islands, large and very small. The coastal region in the south is called **Dalmatia**. The **Dalmatian**, the breed of dog with black spots, is named after it.

**Plitvice Lakes National Park** is the best-known national park in Croatia. There **16 lakes** lie one behind the other, linked by many **waterfalls**. Depending on the light, the water glows green or blue. The park is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Visitors walk on wooden walkways right over the water.

In **Split**, about 1700 years ago, the Roman emperor **Diocletian** had a huge palace built. Around the year 305 he retired there. Later the inhabitants built their houses into the walls, and so today the palace forms the **old town**. **Dubrovnik** with its mighty city wall is also world famous.

Croatia belonged to Yugoslavia for a long time. On **25 June 1991** it declared its **independence**. A war followed that lasted until 1995. On **1 July 2013** Croatia joined the **European Union**, the second successor state of Yugoslavia to do so after Slovenia. The coat of arms shows a **red and white chessboard**, which you can also see on the flag.

About 400 years ago, Croatian soldiers wore knotted neckcloths. This became the **cravat**, and the word comes from “Croat”. Since **1 January 2023** people in Croatia pay with the **euro**. Before that the **kuna** was the currency of the country.

gewusst: The word cravat comes from the Croatian soldiers who wore neckcloths.
People still live today in the walls of Diocletian's Palace in Split.
The Dalmatian is named after a region in Croatia.

teile.einleitung: An offshore wind farm is a group of wind turbines standing in the sea off the coast. There the wind blows more strongly and steadily than on land, so a lot of electricity can be generated.
wichtigste: “Offshore” means “away from the coast”.
The first offshore wind farm in the world was built in 1991 in Denmark.
The first German offshore wind farm is called alpha ventus and went into operation in 2010.
The United Kingdom has the largest offshore wind capacity in Europe.
The electricity reaches land through subsea cables on the sea floor.
The North Sea is especially suitable because of strong wind and shallow water.

abschnitte.text: An **offshore wind farm** consists of many wind turbines that stand on **foundations** in the sea floor. Over the sea there are no hills, houses or forests to slow the wind. That is why it blows more strongly and **more steadily** than on land. The **North Sea** is especially suitable because in many places it is **shallow** and foundations are easy to build.

The first offshore wind farm in the world was called **Vindeby**. It was built in **1991** off the coast of **Denmark** and had eleven turbines. It was in operation until 2017. In Germany the **alpha ventus** wind farm was connected to the grid in **2010**. It lies about 45 kilometres north of the island of **Borkum** and served as a test field for later large wind farms.

The turbines are connected by cables to a **transformer platform**. There the electricity is converted so that it can be carried over long distances. After that **subsea cables** on the sea floor carry the electricity ashore into the **power grid**. Construction and maintenance need special ships and ports such as **Esbjerg** in Denmark.

Off the coast of the **United Kingdom** stand some of the largest wind farms in the world, for example **Hornsea**. As of 2024 the country had the largest capacity in Europe, with Germany second. On the **Dogger Bank** sandbank, about 130 kilometres off the English coast, a wind farm is being built in several stages that is meant to become the largest in the world.

Offshore wind farms generate electricity without exhaust gases and supply a lot of energy. But building in the sea is **expensive** and difficult, and salt water and storms put strain on the installations. Conservationists make sure that sea creatures and birds are disturbed as little as possible. Companies from countries without a sea, such as Switzerland, also take part in such projects.

gewusst: Esbjerg used to be mainly a fishing and oil port and is now a centre for wind farms.
The Dogger Bank is in some places only 15 to 36 metres deep, although it lies far out at sea.

teile.einleitung: Klaksvík is the second largest town in the Faroe Islands, a group of islands in the North Atlantic. It lies on the island of Borðoy and is an important fishing port. The largest town and capital of the Faroe Islands is Tórshavn.
wichtigste: Klaksvík is the second largest town in the Faroe Islands.
The town lies on the island of Borðoy.
It is an important fishing port.
The capital and largest town of the Faroe Islands is Tórshavn.
The Faroe Islands belong to the Kingdom of Denmark, but largely govern themselves.

abschnitte.text: The **Faroe Islands** are a group of 18 islands in the North Atlantic, between Scotland, Norway and Iceland. They belong to the **Kingdom of Denmark**, but have a parliament of their own and manage most things themselves. The people speak **Faroese**, a Nordic language related to Icelandic. The islands are mountainous and green and almost without trees.

Klaksvík lies on the island of **Borðoy** in the north-east of the Faroe Islands. The town lies on a sheltered bay that forms a good **natural harbour**. **Fishing** is very important for Klaksvík, as is the processing of fish. For the Faroe Islands as a whole, fish is the most important export.

In the Faroe Islands many **tunnels** link the islands, and some even run under the sea. One such undersea tunnel links Borðoy with the neighbouring island of Eysturoy. This means you can reach the capital **Tórshavn** from Klaksvík by car. In the past you had to rely on ferries for this.

gewusst: There are clearly more sheep than people in the Faroe Islands, and the name Faroe probably means “sheep islands”.

teile.einleitung: The Lofoten are a group of islands off the coast of northern Norway. Steep mountains rise straight out of the sea, and for centuries cod has been dried here to make stockfish.
wichtigste: The Lofoten lie in northern Norway, north of the Arctic Circle.
The islands are known for steep, pointed mountains right by the sea.
In winter large shoals of cod come to the islands.
The fish is dried in the open air on wooden racks to make stockfish.
Thanks to a warm ocean current, the climate is milder than expected.

abschnitte.text: The Lofoten consist of several large and many small islands. They lie in the county of **Nordland**, north of the **Arctic Circle**. From a distance they look like a wall of pointed peaks rising straight out of the water. In between lie bays, sandy beaches and small fishing villages.

Every winter large shoals of **cod** migrate from the Barents Sea to the Lofoten. For centuries the fishermen here have caught this fish. It is gutted and hung up outdoors on tall **wooden racks**. Cold, dry air dries it over weeks until it is as hard as a board. This **stockfish** keeps for a very long time and was sold as far as southern Europe as early as the Middle Ages.

Typical are the red wooden houses on stilts at the water's edge, the **rorbuer**. In the past fishermen lived in them during the fishing season, and today often holiday guests. A warm ocean current from the south ensures that the sea does not freeze in winter and that the climate is milder than in other places so far north.

Because the Lofoten lie north of the Arctic Circle, in summer the Sun does not set for several weeks. This is called the **midnight sun**. In winter, on the other hand, it stays dark for a long time. Then, when the sky is clear, you can often see the **northern lights**, green ribbons of light that move across the sky.

gewusst: One of the villages on the Lofoten is called just “Å”, one of the shortest place names in the world.
Stockfish needs no salt and no refrigerator, and is preserved only by wind and cold.

teile.einleitung: The Canary Islands, or Canaries for short, are a group of islands in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Africa. They belong to Spain and were formed by volcanoes. Because of the mild climate, many people travel there all year round.
wichtigste: The Canaries lie in the Atlantic off Africa, about 100 kilometres west of Morocco.
They belong to Spain.
There are seven larger main islands.
Tenerife is the largest island, and the volcano Teide stands there.
Teide is 3715 metres high and the highest mountain in Spain.
The islands were formed by volcanic eruptions.
In 2021 a volcano erupted on La Palma and destroyed over a thousand buildings.

abschnitte.text: The Canaries lie in the **Atlantic Ocean**, not far from Morocco. Politically they belong to **Spain** and form an autonomous region of their own there. The seven larger islands are Tenerife, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. There are also some small islands. The largest island is **Tenerife**, where most of the people live as well.

The islands grew out of the sea through **volcanic eruptions**. That is why there is a lot of black **lava rock** and dark sand. On Tenerife stands **Teide**, at 3715 metres the highest mountain in Spain. In **Timanfaya** National Park on Lanzarote there are many volcanic cones, and in some places the ground is still very hot.

The volcanoes are still active today. In **2021** a volcano erupted on **La Palma** in the Cumbre Vieja area. The eruption lasted about three months. Lava flows destroyed over a thousand buildings, as well as roads and fields. Many residents had to leave their homes.

The artist **César Manrique** campaigned on **Lanzarote** for houses to fit in with the volcanic landscape and not to be built too high. There he created special places such as the **Jameos del Agua**, which are built into a lava cave. To this day low white houses shape the look of the island.

It is mild on the Canaries all year round, so they are also called the “islands of eternal spring”. Many tourists, including some from Switzerland, spend their holidays there. The wild ancestor of the **canary** lives on the islands. It is rather greenish, and the yellow canaries were bred by humans.

gewusst: Measured from the sea floor, Teide is one of the highest volcanoes on Earth.
On La Gomera there is a whistled language called Silbo, which people use to communicate across valleys.

teile.einleitung: Copenhagen is the capital of Denmark and the largest city in the country. It lies on the island of Zealand on the Øresund. The city is known for its colourful houses, Tivoli and its many cycle paths.
wichtigste: Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark.
The city lies on the island of Zealand.
The Danish name København means “merchants' harbour”.
The royal family lives in Amalienborg Palace.
The amusement park Tivoli opened in 1843.
Very many people cycle to work.
On the other side of the Øresund lies the Swedish city of Malmö.

abschnitte.text: Copenhagen lies on the island of **Zealand**, the largest island in Denmark proper. Even in the Middle Ages the city was an important **trading place** on the **Øresund**, the strait between Denmark and Sweden. That is why the Danish name **København** means “merchants' harbour”. On the other side lies the Swedish city of **Malmö**. By train the journey there takes only about 35 to 40 minutes.

The Danish **royal family** lives in **Amalienborg** Palace. It consists of four identical palaces around an octagonal square. Every day a **changing of the guard** takes place there. **Nyhavn**, which means “New Harbour”, is also well known. There coloured houses stand by the water, and old wooden ships lie in the canal.

In the middle of the city lies the amusement park **Tivoli**. It opened in **1843** and is one of the oldest amusement parks in the world. There are rides, gardens, concerts and many lights in the evening. Tivoli is one of the best-known tourist attractions in Denmark.

Copenhagen has many wide **cycle paths**, and a large share of people ride a **bicycle** to work or school every day. As early as **1962** the shopping street **Strøget** was closed to cars, and it became one of the first long pedestrian zones in Europe. The success encouraged the city to redesign more streets and squares for pedestrians and bicycles.

Since **1947** Copenhagen has been growing according to the **Finger Plan**. The city is meant to spread like the fingers of a hand along **suburban railway lines**. Between the fingers, **green wedges** with meadows and woods are kept free. This means that from many homes you can quickly reach the station and nature. Swiss cities today also plan in a similar way, putting housing as close as possible to public transport.

gewusst: The small bronze figure of the Little Mermaid at the harbour recalls a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen.
Since the year 2000 the Øresund Bridge has linked Copenhagen and Malmö for cars and trains.

teile.einleitung: HafenCity is a new district of Hamburg that is being built on old port areas on the River Elbe. Its most famous building is the Elbphilharmonie, which was designed by an architecture firm from Basel. Right next to it lies the historic Speicherstadt.
wichtigste: HafenCity is being built on about 157 hectares of former port area in Hamburg.
The Elbphilharmonie comes from the Basel firm Herzog & de Meuron.
It was built on the old Kaispeicher A and opened in January 2017.
The cost to the city rose from a planned 77 million to around 789 million euros.
To protect against storm surges, the buildings stand on raised mounds called warften.
The neighbouring Speicherstadt has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

abschnitte.titel: A new district by the water
abschnitte.text: **HafenCity** is being built on about **157 hectares** of former port area at the Grasbrook in **Hamburg**. It is one of the largest inner-city development projects in Europe. Where ships used to be loaded, flats, offices, schools and parks are being built. Since **2012** the underground line **U4** has run to HafenCity, and in 2018 it was extended as far as the Elbbrücken.

The best-known building in HafenCity is the **Elbphilharmonie**. It was designed by the **Basel** architecture firm **Herzog & de Meuron**. They set a glass concert hall on top of an old warehouse, the brick **Kaispeicher A**. Between the old base and the new glass building, at a height of about 37 metres, lies a public **plaza** with a view. The concert hall opened in **January 2017**.

Originally **77 million euros** had been planned for the Elbphilharmonie. According to the Hamburg Senate, the cost to the city finally rose to about **789 million euros**, roughly ten times as much. That is why it counts as an example of **cost explosions** in big projects. At the Elbbrücken, the 245 metre high **Elbtower** was also supposed to be built. When the investor's Signa group declared insolvency at the end of 2023, the building site came to a standstill.

HafenCity lies right on the **Elbe** and outside the big dykes. In **storm surges** the water can rise a great deal. That is why the buildings stand on raised hills, the **warften**, up to about 7.5 metres above standard elevation zero. The **promenades** by the water, on the other hand, are allowed to flood.

The **Speicherstadt** borders directly on HafenCity. It was built from **1883** for the free port and is the largest historic **warehouse complex** in the world. The red brick buildings stand on piles in the water. Since **2015** the Speicherstadt, together with the Kontorhaus district and the **Chilehaus**, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: The Elbphilharmonie was designed by an architecture firm from Basel.
The plaza of the Elbphilharmonie is public and offers a panoramic view over the port.

teile.einleitung: The Lipizzaner is a famous breed of horse. It is named after the Lipica stud farm in present-day Slovenia. They are best known from the Spanish Riding School in Vienna.
wichtigste: The Lipizzaners are named after the Lipica stud farm in Slovenia.
The Lipica stud farm was founded in 1580.
Most Lipizzaners are white.
The foals are born dark and only turn white over the years.
They perform at the Spanish Riding School in Vienna.

abschnitte.titel: A stud farm in the Karst
abschnitte.text: A **stud farm** is an establishment where horses are bred. The **Lipica** stud farm was founded in **1580**. At that time the area belonged to the realm of the **Habsburgs**, and today Lipica lies in **Slovenia**, near the border with Italy. The breed of the **Lipizzaners** is named after this place. The stud farm is among the oldest in the world.

Most Lipizzaners are **white**, and are also called **greys**. But their **foals** are born dark, almost black or brown. Only over several years does their coat grow lighter and lighter. Lipizzaners are strong, quick to learn and well suited to difficult exercises.

The Lipizzaners from the **Spanish Riding School** in **Vienna** are famous. There riders and horses have shown **classical horsemanship** for centuries. The displays also include jumps in which the horse rises into the air. The horses for Vienna now come from the **Piber** stud farm in Styria in Austria.

gewusst: A Lipizzaner is born dark and only turns white after a few years.
The Lipica stud farm is over 440 years old.

teile.einleitung: An esker is a long, narrow ridge of gravel and sand that formed in the ice age. In Swedish it is called an os, plural oser. There are especially many in Finland and Sweden.
wichtigste: An esker is a long, narrow ridge of gravel from the ice age.
It formed from gravel deposited by meltwater rivers under the glacier.
Eskers can be many kilometres long.
In Finland many eskers run between lakes.
A well-known example is Punkaharju on Lake Saimaa.

abschnitte.text: In the **ice age** thick **glaciers** lay over northern Europe. Under and inside the ice, **meltwater rivers** flowed as if in tunnels. They carried **gravel** and **sand** with them and deposited it. When the ice melted, the gravel stayed behind as a long, narrow ridge. This ridge is called an **esker**, in Swedish **os**, with the plural **oser**. The word comes from Swedish.

In **Finland** and **Sweden** there are especially many eskers. They often run like causeways between **lakes**. Pine trees grow on them, and roads often run over them. A well-known example is **Punkaharju** in the **Saimaa** lake district. Because eskers consist of gravel, they store good **groundwater** and are also used for gravel pits.

In Switzerland too, ice age glaciers shaped the landscape. Often you see **moraines**, ridges of debris that the glacier pushed in front of it or left at its edge. An esker, by contrast, was deposited by **water**. That is why its gravel is rounded and sorted by size.

gewusst: Some eskers are over a hundred kilometres long, if you add up their sections.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the Hanseatic League was an alliance of merchants and towns in the north of Europe. Together they controlled trade on the Baltic Sea and the North Sea for a long time. Traces of it can still be seen in many towns today.
wichtigste: The Hanseatic League was an alliance of merchants and trading towns.
For a long time it controlled trade on the Baltic Sea.
Important Hanseatic towns were Lübeck, Hamburg, Danzig and Visby.
Goods traded included fish, salt, grain and furs.
Lübeck was regarded as the most important town of the League.
Its typical ship was the cog.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages travelling was dangerous. Merchants therefore joined together to protect themselves on the road and in foreign towns. The word **Hanse** originally means “group” or “band”. Later whole towns joined together in this alliance. Their representatives met at assemblies, the **Hansetage**, and discussed common rules there.

At times very many towns belonged to the League, mainly on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. The most important was **Lübeck**, which was called the “Queen of the Hanse”. Others included Hamburg, Bremen, Rostock, Danzig, Riga and **Visby** on the island of Gotland. Towns inland, such as Cologne, were also members. Many of these places have magnificent brick churches and town halls that tell of the wealth of the Hanseatic period.

The best-known ship of the League was the **cog**, a broad sailing ship with plenty of room for cargo. The merchants carried **fish** such as herring and stockfish, **salt**, **grain**, timber, wax and **furs** from place to place. Salt was especially important, because it could be used to preserve fish. Abroad, the League had large trading posts, the **Kontore**, for example in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Hanseatic League
abschnitte.text: The League was at its most powerful in the 14th and 15th centuries. After that the territorial princes and new trading powers such as the Netherlands and England grew stronger. New sea routes to America and Asia also changed trade. Little by little the alliance lost importance. The last Hansetag took place in the 17th century.

Some towns still proudly carry the title **Hanseatic City** in their names, such as Hamburg, Bremen and Lübeck. You can even see it on German car number plates: HH stands for Hansestadt Hamburg, HB for Hansestadt Bremen and HL for Hansestadt Lübeck. Since 1980 there has also been a league of towns again that recalls the old Hanseatic League and promotes culture and partnership.

gewusst: The Holstentor in Lübeck is one of the best-known buildings from the Hanseatic period.
The Hanseatic quarter of Bryggen in Bergen in Norway is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Sea Organ in Zadar in Croatia is a musical instrument played by the sea. Waves push air through pipes under stone steps on the shore and so produce notes.
wichtigste: The Sea Organ stands in the town of Zadar in Croatia.
It opened in 2005.
Under wide stone steps on the shore lie pipes.
The waves push air through the pipes, and so notes are made.
The music sounds different every moment, depending on the waves.

abschnitte.text: On the shore of **Zadar**, wide steps of stone lead into the sea. Under them lie many **pipes**. When a wave comes in, it pushes air into the pipes. The air flows up through openings in the steps and produces **notes**, similar to a church organ. Because no wave is like another, the music never repeats exactly.

The Sea Organ opened in **2005**. It was designed by the architect **Nikola Bašić**. Before that the shore at this spot was a rather grey concrete wall. Today many people sit here on the steps, listen and look out to sea. The installation has won a European prize for the design of public spaces.

Right next to it lies another work by the same architect: the **Greeting to the Sun**. This is a large circle of glass panels set in the ground with **solar cells**. By day they collect solar energy, and at night the circle glows in bright colours. The place is especially popular at **sunset**.

gewusst: When the sea is calm the organ sings softly, and in storms and high waves it becomes much louder.

teile.einleitung: Kyiv is the capital of Ukraine and lies on the River Dnipro. The city is over a thousand years old and was once the centre of Kyivan Rus. It is famous for its churches with golden domes.
wichtigste: Kyiv is the capital and largest city of Ukraine.
The city lies on the River Dnipro.
From the 9th century Kyiv was the centre of Kyivan Rus.
St Sophia's Cathedral from the 11th century is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Kyiv Pechersk Lavra is also a World Heritage Site.
The central square is called the Maidan, which means Independence Square.

abschnitte.text: Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in eastern Europe. From the 9th century it was the centre of **Kyivan Rus**, a great East Slavic realm. Around the year 988 Prince Vladimir adopted **Christianity**. Ukraine, Russia and Belarus all see Kyivan Rus as part of their history.

A landmark of the city is **St Sophia's Cathedral**. It was built in the 11th century and has golden domes. Inside there are very old **mosaics** and wall paintings. Together with the Pechersk Lavra, it is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The **Kyiv Pechersk Lavra**, or Cave Monastery, was founded in the 11th century on the slope above the Dnipro. The first **monks** lived in underground passages and caves. Later large churches and bell towers were added. To this day many believers and tourists visit the caves with candles in their hands.

The central square is called **Maidan Nezalezhnosti**, which means **Independence Square**. The name recalls Ukraine's independence of 1991. The square was the scene of large **demonstrations** several times, for example in 2004 and from 2013 to 2014. Since the Russian attack on Ukraine in 2022, Kyiv too has been affected by the war.

gewusst: The Arsenalna metro station in Kyiv is one of the deepest in the world, lying more than 100 metres underground.
In Ukrainian the city is called Kyiv.

teile.einleitung: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain range in Greece. In the old Greek legends the most important gods lived there with their king Zeus.
wichtigste: The highest peak is called Mytikas and is about 2918 metres high.
According to the legends twelve main gods lived on Olympus.
Zeus was the king of the gods and hurled lightning bolts when he was angry.
Poseidon ruled over the sea.
In 1913 two Genevans with a Greek first climbed the highest peak.
In 1938 Olympus became the first national park in Greece.

abschnitte.text: Olympus lies in the north of Greece, not far from the sea. Its highest peak is called **Mytikas**, which means roughly “nose”. It is about **2918 metres** high. That is a lot for Greece, but less than some Swiss mountains. The **Matterhorn**, at about 4478 metres, is much higher, while the Rigi, Pilatus and Säntis are lower than Olympus.

The ancient Greeks believed that their most important gods lived on Olympus. People speak of the **twelve Olympian gods**. Their king was **Zeus**, the god of the sky and the weather. When he was angry, he hurled **lightning bolts**. The Olympians also included **Hera**, **Athena** and **Apollo**.

**Poseidon** was the god of the sea. He carried a **trident**, a fork with three points. With it, according to the legends, he could stir up waves and earthquakes. Many stories about the gods of Olympus are still known today from books, films and games.

For a long time nobody stood on the highest peak. In **1913** the two **Genevans** **Frédéric Boissonnas** and **Daniel Baud-Bovy**, together with the Greek **Christos Kakkalos**, were the first to reach it. So the first climbers came partly from **Switzerland**. Today many people hike up Olympus every year.

In **1938** the area around Olympus was declared the first **national park** in Greece. Many rare **plants** grow there, and some occur only here. Later Olympus was also designated a UNESCO biosphere reserve.

gewusst: The Olympic Games are not named after Mount Olympus, but after the sanctuary of Olympia on the Peloponnese.
Frédéric Boissonnas was a photographer and took many well-known pictures on his travels in Greece.

teile.einleitung: The midnight sun is the Sun that, in summer north of the Arctic Circle, does not set even at midnight. The reason is the tilt of the Earth's axis.
wichtigste: The Arctic Circle lies at about 66.6 degrees north.
North of it the Sun does not set at least once a year.
The cause is the tilt of the Earth's axis of about 23.4 degrees.
In Longyearbyen on Svalbard the midnight sun lasts about four months.
The Arctic Circle moves about 14.5 metres north every year.
In Saint Petersburg there are the White Nights, but no midnight sun.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Sun does not set
abschnitte.text: The Earth's axis is tilted by about **23.4 degrees**. In summer the northern hemisphere is therefore turned towards the Sun. Near the North Pole the Sun then stays above the horizon around the clock. The boundary beyond which this happens at least once a year is the **Arctic Circle** at about **66 degrees 34 minutes north**. In winter it is the other way round: then there is the **polar night**, in which the Sun does not rise at all.

You can even see the midnight sun a little **south** of the Arctic Circle. The **atmosphere** bends the light near the horizon, and the disc of the Sun has a certain size. That is why the Sun remains visible up to about 80 to 100 kilometres south of the Arctic Circle. The further north you go, the longer the period without a sunset lasts. In **Longyearbyen** on Svalbard, at about 78 degrees north, it is about **four months**, from about mid April to the end of August.

At **Rovaniemi**, the capital of Lapland in Finland, the Arctic Circle runs right through the well-known Father Christmas village. In Norway, on the bare plateau of **Saltfjellet** on the E6 road, there is an Arctic Circle Centre. In Iceland the Arctic Circle crosses only the small island of **Grímsey**, about 40 kilometres off the north coast.

The tilt of the Earth's axis is at present slowly decreasing. As a result the Arctic Circle shifts about **14.5 metres** north every year. On Grímsey a work of art that marks the line is therefore moved again and again. Over very long periods the tilt of the Earth's axis swings back and forth.

**Saint Petersburg** lies at about 60 degrees north, south of the Arctic Circle. There the Sun sets briefly in summer, but it does not get properly dark. These bright summer nights are called **White Nights**. In Switzerland the longest day in June is about 16 hours long, but after that it gets completely dark at night.

gewusst: During the midnight sun you can read a book outdoors at midnight without a lamp.
At the South Pole the midnight sun also exists, only in exactly the opposite season.

teile.einleitung: The Hallgrímskirkja is the big church on a hill in the middle of Reykjavík, the capital of Iceland. With its tall tower it can be seen from far away and is regarded as a landmark of the city.
wichtigste: The Hallgrímskirkja stands in Reykjavík in Iceland.
It is about 75 metres high and one of the tallest buildings in Iceland.
Its shape is reminiscent of columns of basalt, a volcanic rock.
It is an Evangelical Lutheran church.
It is named after the poet Hallgrímur Pétursson.

abschnitte.titel: A church that looks as if it grew out of stone
abschnitte.text: The tower of the Hallgrímskirkja rises in steps, like a staircase of grey columns. The architect **Guðjón Samúelsson** took his inspiration from **basalt columns**. Columns like these form in Iceland when lava cools slowly. The building took a very long time: it began in the 1940s and was only completely finished in the 1980s. From the tower there is a wide view over the colourful roofs of Reykjavík.

The church bears the name of **Hallgrímur Pétursson**, an Icelandic pastor and poet of the 17th century. His hymns are still very well known in Iceland today. Inside, the church is bright and simple. Especially striking is the large **organ** with several thousand pipes. Services and concerts take place in the church.

abschnitte.titel: The statue in front of the church
abschnitte.text: In front of the church stands a statue of the seafarer **Leif Eriksson**. According to the old sagas, he was one of the first Europeans to reach North America, around the year 1000. The statue was a gift from the USA to Iceland. Many visitors first see the statue and then climb the tower.

gewusst: The Hallgrímskirkja is so tall that you can see it from almost anywhere in Reykjavík.
Iceland has a very small population, so a building 75 metres tall is something very special there.

teile.einleitung: Under the floor of the North Sea lie large deposits of oil and natural gas. They have been extracted since the end of the 1960s and have made Norway and Great Britain in particular rich.
wichtigste: In 1969 Ekofisk, the first large oil field in the Norwegian part of the North Sea, was discovered.
From 1971 oil flowed there.
The crude oil grade Brent is named after a British oil field and is an important benchmark for the oil price.
Aberdeen in Scotland and Stavanger in Norway are centres of the oil industry.
Norway saves its oil revenues in the largest sovereign wealth fund in the world.
British production peaked in 1999 and has declined since.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people did not believe that much oil lay under the North Sea. At the end of **1969** the company Phillips Petroleum discovered the **Ekofisk** field in the Norwegian part. From **1971** oil was extracted there. This marked the start of Norway's **oil age**. Soon afterwards large fields were also found in the British part, for example in 1971 the **Brent field** east of the Shetland Islands.

The oil from the Brent field gave its name to an important **benchmark grade**. A benchmark grade is an oil whose price many other deals are based on. When the news speaks of the oil price, the price of **Brent** is often meant. It also affects how much petrol and heating oil cost in Switzerland.

**Aberdeen** in Scotland is regarded as the oil capital of Europe. From there the platforms are supplied by helicopters and ships. In **Stavanger** many oil companies and the Norwegian oil authority have their seat, and there is an oil museum. **Norway** invests its oil revenues in a **sovereign wealth fund**. It owns shares in thousands of companies around the world and is also meant to serve future generations.

In 1988 a gas explosion and a major fire occurred on the **Piper Alpha** platform off Scotland. 167 people died. It is the worst accident in offshore oil production. Afterwards the safety rules were greatly tightened. In 1995 a company wanted to sink the disused oil storage buoy **Brent Spar** in the Atlantic. After protests from **Greenpeace** and many customers, it was dismantled on land.

In the British part production peaked in **1999**. Since then many fields have been largely **depleted**, that is, mostly empty. Old platforms have to be dismantled, which costs a lot of money. At the same time more and more **wind farms** are being built in the North Sea.

gewusst: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is the largest in the world.
The platforms in the North Sea are among the largest structures that people have ever placed in the sea.

teile.einleitung: In most countries cars drive on the right, but in some they drive on the left. This is called left-hand traffic. Great Britain is especially well known for it.
wichtigste: In Great Britain and Ireland people drive on the left.
In Switzerland and most countries in Europe people drive on the right.
With left-hand traffic the steering wheel is usually on the right.
Bicycles in London also ride on the left.
Australia and Japan also drive on the left.
In London “Look right” is often painted on the road.

abschnitte.text: In **Switzerland** cars drive on the right-hand side of the road. This is called **right-hand traffic**. In **Great Britain** it is the other way round: people drive on the left, and **left-hand traffic** applies. On the whole island of **Ireland** people also drive on the left, in **Northern Ireland** just as in the **Republic of Ireland**. In Europe Malta and Cyprus also drive on the left.

abschnitte.titel: The steering wheel on the other side
abschnitte.text: In British cars the **steering wheel is on the right**. Because people drive on the left, the driver sits closer to the **middle of the road**. From there he can see oncoming traffic better and overtake more safely. In Swiss cars the steering wheel is therefore on the left.

Anyone coming from Switzerland looks **left** first when crossing the road, out of habit. In London, however, cars come from the **right** first. That is why many pedestrian crossings have **“Look right”** painted on the road. **Cyclists** also keep to left-hand traffic and ride on the left like the cars.

It is not only in Great Britain that people drive on the left. In **Australia**, New Zealand, India and **Japan** left-hand traffic also applies. In many of these countries this comes from their long connection with **Great Britain**. Some countries have also switched: **Sweden** changed from left-hand to right-hand traffic in 1967 on a single day.

gewusst: Sweden switched from left-hand to right-hand traffic overnight in 1967.
In Great Britain bicycles ride on the left too.

teile.einleitung: In Europe farming is done in very different ways, depending on climate and soil. In the south olives and vegetables grow, in the east a lot of grain, and in the mountains cows graze. The EU supports its farmers with a common policy.
wichtigste: France produces the agricultural goods of the greatest value in the EU.
The small Netherlands is among the largest agricultural exporters in the world.
Ukraine is called the “breadbasket of Europe”.
Spain is the largest producer of olive oil in the world.
Since 1962 the EU has supported its agriculture with the Common Agricultural Policy.
In the Swiss mountain region dairy and cattle farming is most widespread.

abschnitte.text: **France** produces the farm products of the **greatest value** within the EU. It has a lot of fertile land and a favourable climate. Much grain, milk, meat and **wine** come from there. The small **Netherlands** is among the largest **agricultural exporters** in the world. It sells a lot of vegetables, **flowers**, dairy products and meat abroad, often from modern **greenhouses**.

**Ukraine** is often called the **“breadbasket of Europe”**. There are wide areas of very fertile **black earth**, a dark soil rich in humus. The country exports a lot of **wheat**, **maize** and **sunflower oil**. Grain from Ukraine is sold to many countries around the world.

**Spain** is the **largest producer of olive oil** in the world. Huge olive groves grow above all in **Andalusia**. In good years almost half of the world's olive oil comes from Spain. In the province of **Almería**, greenhouses of plastic sheeting cover more than 300 square kilometres. The area is called the **“sea of plastic”**, and from there comes a lot of vegetables for the whole of Europe.

In the Netherlands a lot of land has been won from the sea. Areas enclosed by dykes like this are called **polders**. They often lie below sea level and are protected by **dykes**. **Pumps** keep the land dry, so that it can be used as fields or pasture.

Since **1962** the EU has supported its farmers with the **Common Agricultural Policy**, or **CAP** for short. It pays subsidies and regulates the agricultural market. It is one of the largest items in the EU budget. Switzerland does not belong to the EU, but also supports its farmers, for example with **direct payments**. In the Swiss mountain region meadows are better suited than fields, which is why **dairy and cattle farming** is widespread there. In summer the cows often graze on the **alp**.

gewusst: A country as small as the Netherlands exports more farm products than almost any other country in the world.
The plastic sea of Almería is so big that you can see it in satellite pictures.

teile.einleitung: The Venetian Lagoon is a shallow bay of the sea on the Adriatic in Italy. In it lies the city of Venice with its canals, and many other islands. The lagoon, together with Venice, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Most of Venice's houses stand on wooden piles.
During “acqua alta” St Mark's Square is under water.
Murano is known for glassblowers, Burano for colourful houses and lace.
