The MOSE protection system has been used against flooding since 2020.
The Venice Film Festival has been held on the Lido since 1932.

abschnitte.text: A **lagoon** is a shallow body of water separated from the open sea by narrow strips of land. In the Venetian Lagoon lie many islands. The city of **Venice** itself is built on over a hundred small islands that are linked by **canals** and bridges. Instead of cars, boats travel there. Venice and its lagoon are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The floor of the lagoon is soft and muddy. That is why **millions of wooden piles** were driven into the ground. Most of Venice's houses stand on them. Under water, where hardly any **oxygen** gets in, the piles hardly rot at all. So they have held for centuries.

**“Acqua alta”** means **high water** in Italian. In storms and high tides the water rises so high that **St Mark's Square** is flooded. The **MOSE** system was built for protection. It consists of movable barriers at the entrances to the lagoon. When flooding threatens, they are raised and hold the sea back. MOSE has been in use since **2020**.

On the island of **Murano** skilful **glass** has been made since the 13th century. The glass furnaces were moved there from the city for **fire safety reasons**. The island of **Burano** is known for its **brightly painted houses**, each in a different strong colour. Fine **bobbin lace** is also made there.

The **Lido** is a long, narrow island between the lagoon and the open sea. There are sandy beaches and seaside resorts here. Every year the **Venice Film Festival** takes place on the Lido. It has existed since **1932** and is regarded as the **oldest film festival in the world**.

gewusst: The wooden piles under Venice have carried the city for hundreds of years.
The glass furnaces came to Murano so that no fires would break out in Venice.

teile.einleitung: Ukraine is one of the most important agricultural countries in the world. Its fertile soils have given it the name “breadbasket of Europe”. Since the war from 2022, exporting grain has become more difficult.
wichtigste: The fertile black earth makes Ukraine the “breadbasket of Europe”.
About 70 per cent of the country's area is used for farming.
Before 2022 Ukraine was the largest exporter of sunflower oil.
Odesa is the most important port for grain exports.
In July 2022 the UN and Turkey brokered a grain deal.
In the Holodomor famine of 1932 and 1933 millions of people died.

abschnitte.text: Large parts of southern and eastern Ukraine were naturally **steppe**, that is, grassland with hot summers and cold winters. Under the steppe grass the **black earth** formed over a long time, called **chernozem** in Russian. This soil is very rich in **humus** and therefore especially fertile. A large part of the world's black earth lies in Ukraine. Today the steppes have been almost entirely turned into farmland.

About **70 per cent** of the country's area is used for farming, one of the highest shares in Europe. The main crops are **wheat**, **maize**, barley and **sunflowers**. Before the war Ukraine supplied about half of the **sunflower oil** traded worldwide. A widespread reading of the flag sees the **sky** in the blue and a **field of grain** in the yellow.

In **1932 and 1933** Ukraine belonged to the **Soviet Union**. The government forced farmers to bring their land into state-controlled farms, which is called **forced collectivisation**. At the same time the state ruthlessly seized grain. In the famine that followed, the **Holodomor**, millions of people died. Many states now recognise it as a **genocide**.

Traditionally most grain is exported through **Odesa** and the neighbouring ports of Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi on the **Black Sea**. After the Russian attack in 2022 the sea route was blocked. In **July 2022** the **UN** and **Turkey** brokered a **grain deal** that allowed safe shipments. In July 2023 Russia withdrew again. As an alternative route, the Danube ports of **Izmail** and **Reni** were greatly expanded.

gewusst: A large part of the most fertile soil in the world lies in Ukraine.
Grain from the Danube ports reaches the Black Sea by way of the Danube.

teile.einleitung: The Moselle is a river that flows through France, Luxembourg and Germany. Its valley is famous for steep vineyards, castles and old Roman towns.
wichtigste: The Moselle rises in the Vosges in France.
It is about 544 kilometres long.
At Koblenz it flows into the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck.
Trier on the Moselle is regarded as the oldest city in Germany.
In the Moselle Valley wine has been grown since Roman times.
In the village of Schengen the Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985.

abschnitte.titel: From the Vosges to the Rhine
abschnitte.text: The **Moselle** rises in the **Vosges** in France. It is about **544 kilometres** long. For a stretch it forms the border between **Luxembourg** and Germany. Near **Konz**, just before Trier, the **Saar** flows into the Moselle. At **Koblenz** the Moselle finally flows into the **Rhine**, the river that also flows through Basel.

The spit of land between the Rhine and the Moselle in Koblenz is called the **Deutsches Eck**, or German Corner. There stands a large monument with an equestrian statue. The place is a well-known **landmark** of Koblenz. Many excursion boats put in here.

**Trier** was founded by the **Romans** and is regarded as the oldest city in Germany. Its best-known building is the **Porta Nigra**, a large Roman city gate of dark stone. Remains of baths and a bridge from Roman times are also preserved. Many of these buildings are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

On the steep slopes of the **Moselle Valley**, **wine** has been grown since Roman times. The most important grape variety is **Riesling**. High above the small town of **Cochem** towers the **Reichsburg**, a popular subject for photographs. Many people hike or cycle along the river.

In the wine-growing village of **Schengen** in Luxembourg, Luxembourg, Germany and France meet. In **1985** the **Schengen Agreement** was signed on a ship on the Moselle. It ensures that you can travel between many countries in Europe without passport checks. **Switzerland** too now belongs to the Schengen area.

gewusst: The Moselle was developed with locks so that large cargo ships can travel on it.
The name Moselle comes from the Latin “Mosella”, which means “little Meuse”.

teile.einleitung: Mezzogiorno is the name for the south of Italy, including Sicily and Sardinia. Since the unification of Italy the south has been economically weaker than the north, which is known as the Southern Question.
wichtigste: “Mezzogiorno” literally means midday, and refers to the south of Italy.
It includes the southern mainland as well as Sicily and Sardinia.
Until 1860 to 1861 most of it belonged to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
The south's lag behind is called the “Questione meridionale”.
Many people emigrated to the north and abroad, including to Switzerland.
Organised crime such as the ’Ndrangheta and the Camorra is a major problem.

abschnitte.text: **Mezzogiorno** means **midday** in Italian. At midday the Sun stands in the south, which is why the word also refers to the south of Italy. It includes the regions of Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Apulia, Basilicata and Calabria, as well as the large islands of **Sicily** and **Sardinia**. Until 1860 to 1861 most of it belonged to the **Kingdom of the Two Sicilies** with its capital **Naples**. After Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand it was absorbed into the Kingdom of Italy.

After the unification of Italy in 1861 a great difference appeared between the richer north and the poorer south. The debate about causes and solutions is called the **Questione meridionale**, the Southern Question. One important reason was **large landed estates**: a few families owned much land, on which day labourers worked. These estates are called **latifundia**. A land reform of 1950 redistributed part of the land.

From 1950 into the 1980s the **Cassa per il Mezzogiorno** supported the south. It paid for roads, irrigation and new factories. Large plants such as the steelworks in **Taranto** created jobs, but hardly attracted smaller businesses. Critics therefore called them **“cathedrals in the desert”**. In 1984 the Cassa was dissolved because its effect fell short of expectations.

Because there was little work in the south, **millions of people** moved away in the 20th century: to Turin and Milan, to the USA or to **Switzerland**. In the 1950s and 1960s many southern Italians worked in Swiss factories and on building sites. Many families stayed and are now firmly part of Switzerland.

A major problem in the south is **organised crime**. The **’Ndrangheta** comes from Calabria and is now regarded as one of the most powerful mafia organisations, also in international drug trafficking. The **Camorra** is a network of clans in Naples and the surrounding area. Police, courts and many brave citizens take a stand against these groups.

gewusst: The name Mezzogiorno comes from the position of the Sun: at midday the Sun is in the south for us.
In Switzerland there are still many families today with roots in Calabria, Apulia or Sicily.

teile.einleitung: Mother Teresa was a Catholic nun who devoted her life to poor and sick people in India. She was born in Skopje in 1910 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
wichtigste: Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910.
Her real name was Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu.
She came from an Albanian family.
In India she helped the poor, the sick and the dying.
In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize.
She died in Kolkata in 1997.

abschnitte.text: Mother Teresa was born in **1910** in **Skopje**, today the capital of North Macedonia. Her real name was **Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu**. She came from an **Albanian** family that was very devout. Even as a young girl she wanted to help other people.

At the age of 18 she joined a Catholic **order**, a community of nuns. Soon afterwards she travelled to **India** and worked there as a teacher. In the city of **Kolkata** she saw how many people lived on the street in great poverty. She decided to devote herself entirely to these people.

Mother Teresa founded an order of her own, the **Missionaries of Charity**. The sisters wear white saris with blue stripes. They nursed the sick, took care of orphans and accompanied the **dying**. Today the order is active in many countries of the world.

In **1979** Mother Teresa received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. She died in **1997** in Kolkata. In 2016 the Catholic Church **canonised** her. There was also criticism of her, for example of the way the sick were cared for in her homes. For many people, however, she remains a model of willingness to help.

gewusst: In Skopje there now stands a memorial house for Mother Teresa, on the spot where her baptismal church once stood.
She is said to have used the Nobel Prize money for the poor instead of holding a celebratory banquet.

teile.einleitung: Montenegro is a small country in south-eastern Europe on the Adriatic. It has high mountains, a deep gorge and a famous bay that looks like a fjord.
wichtigste: Montenegro means “black mountain”, and in Montenegrin the country is called Crna Gora.
The capital is Podgorica.
Since 2006 Montenegro has been a state of its own.
The country lies on the Adriatic.
People pay with the euro, although Montenegro is not in the EU.
The Tara Gorge is over 1300 metres deep in places.
Montenegro shares Lake Skadar with Albania.

abschnitte.text: The name **Montenegro** is Italian and means **“black mountain”**. In the national language the country is called **Crna Gora**, which means the same. The name probably comes from the dark forests on the mountains. Montenegro is very mountainous, and it has fewer inhabitants than the canton of Zurich.

The capital and largest city is **Podgorica**. For a long time Montenegro was joined with **Serbia** in a common state. In **2006** the people voted in a referendum for **independence**. People pay with the **euro**, although Montenegro does not belong to the European Union.

abschnitte.titel: Coast and the Bay of Kotor
abschnitte.text: Montenegro has a coast on the **Adriatic** with beaches and old little towns. Especially famous is the **Bay of Kotor**. It reaches far inland, and steep mountains rise straight out of the water. The old town of **Kotor** with its town walls is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the north the River **Tara** has cut deep into the rock. The **Tara Gorge** is over **1300 metres** deep in places and is among the deepest gorges in Europe. In the south lies **Lake Skadar** on the border with **Albania**. It is the largest lake on the Balkan Peninsula and an important habitat for birds such as the Dalmatian pelican.

gewusst: The Tara Gorge belongs to Durmitor National Park, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Montenegro is roughly a third the size of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Lake Ohrid lies in south-eastern Europe on the border between North Macedonia and Albania. It is regarded as one of the oldest lakes in Europe and is known for its special animals and its old town.
wichtigste: Lake Ohrid lies between North Macedonia and Albania.
It is probably over a million years old.
Many animal species live in it that exist nowhere else.
The water is very clear and the lake is deep.
The lake and the town of Ohrid are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Most lakes in Europe, including many in Switzerland, formed after the last **ice age** and so are a few thousand years old. **Lake Ohrid** is much older, probably over **a million years**. It lies in a rift between mountains that formed slowly. Its water is very **clear**, and at its deepest point the lake is almost 300 metres deep.

Because the lake is so old, species of its own were able to develop here over a long time. Many snails, crustaceans and fish occur **only in Lake Ohrid**. Such species are called **endemic**. The **Ohrid trout** is well known. Researchers from many countries study the lake to learn more about the history of nature.

On the shore in North Macedonia lies the town of **Ohrid** with many old **churches** and monasteries. In the Middle Ages the town was an important centre of Christianity and learning in the Balkans. The lake and the town are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Today many people holiday here.

gewusst: Lake Ohrid is among the oldest lakes in the world that still exist today.
Later the Albanian part of the lake was also added to the World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Iberian Peninsula lies in the far south-west of Europe. Mainly Spain and Portugal lie on it, together with the small state of Andorra and the British territory of Gibraltar. In the north the Pyrenees separate the peninsula from the rest of Europe.
wichtigste: Mainly Spain and Portugal lie on the Iberian Peninsula.
It is surrounded by the Atlantic and the Mediterranean.
The longest river is the Tagus, at over 1000 kilometres.
In the middle of Spain lies the high plateau of the Meseta.
It gets its name from the ancient people of the Iberians.
Spain is about five times as large as Portugal.
Portugal has only one neighbouring country: Spain.

abschnitte.text: The Iberian Peninsula is surrounded by water on three sides. In the west and north lies the **Atlantic**, and in the east and south the **Mediterranean**. In the north-east the **Pyrenees** link the peninsula with the rest of the mainland. In the far south, Africa is separated only by the narrow **Strait of Gibraltar**, which is only about 14 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. On clear days you can see Morocco from Spain.

**Spain** takes up the largest part of the peninsula and is about five times as large as Portugal. **Portugal** lies in the west on the Atlantic. It has only a single neighbouring country, namely Spain. In the Pyrenees lies the small state of **Andorra**. In the far south, **Gibraltar** with its famous rock belongs to Great Britain.

In the middle of Spain lies the **Meseta**, a wide, high-lying plain. There the summers are hot and dry and the winters are often cold. The capital Madrid also lies on this plateau. The longest river of the peninsula is the **Tagus**. It is over 1000 kilometres long, flows from Spain through Portugal and reaches the Atlantic at **Lisbon**. Other large rivers are the Ebro, the Douro and the Guadalquivir.

The peninsula gets its name from the **Iberians**. This people lived over 2000 years ago in the east and south of the peninsula. Later the **Romans** conquered the area and called it Hispania, which became the name Spain. From the year 711 the **Moors**, Muslims from North Africa, ruled large parts of it. Magnificent buildings such as the **Alhambra** in Granada date from this time. By 1492 Christian kingdoms had won back the whole area.

gewusst: From Spain you can take a ferry to Africa in about an hour.
The only wild monkeys in Europe, the Barbary macaques, live on the Rock of Gibraltar.

teile.einleitung: The Päijänne is a large lake in the south of Finland. It is the second largest lake in the country. From it the capital, Helsinki, gets its drinking water through a long tunnel.
wichtigste: The Päijänne is the second largest lake in Finland.
It is long and narrow and lies in the south of the country.
A rock tunnel about 120 kilometres long brings its water to Helsinki.
The water of the lake is very clean.
Finland is often called the “Land of a Thousand Lakes”.

abschnitte.text: The **Päijänne** is a long lake with many bays and islands. It stretches from the town of **Jyväskylä** in the north to near **Lahti** in the south. Only Saimaa is larger in Finland. Finland has tens of thousands of lakes and is therefore often called the **Land of a Thousand Lakes**. Many of them formed when the glaciers melted after the last **ice age**.

The capital, **Helsinki**, needs a lot of clean water. That is why the Finns built a **tunnel** about **120 kilometres** long through solid rock, the **Päijänne Tunnel**. Through it the water of the lake flows as far as the capital region. There it is treated further and then distributed. The tunnel is among the longest tunnels in the world, and the Gotthard Base Tunnel, at 57 kilometres, is only half as long.

Around the lake lie forests, rocks and many holiday homes. In summer people go out in boats and canoes, swim or fish. In winter the lake often freezes over. Part of the area is protected as a **national park**.

gewusst: A large part of the people in the Helsinki area drink water from the Päijänne.
The Päijänne Tunnel is more than twice as long as the Gotthard Base Tunnel.

teile.einleitung: Normandy is a region in the north-west of France on the English Channel. It is known for its history with the Normans, the Allied landings in 1944, and for cheese, apples and art.
wichtigste: Normandy takes its name from the Normans, Vikings from the north.
In 1066 Duke William the Conqueror conquered England.
The Bayeux Tapestry tells this conquest in pictures.
On 6 June 1944, “D-Day”, the Allies landed on the beaches of Normandy.
The cheese Camembert is named after a village in Normandy.
The painter Claude Monet laid out his water lily pond in Giverny.

abschnitte.text: In the **10th century** **Vikings** from Scandinavia settled on the Seine. They were called **Normans**, meaning “Northmen”. Their leader Rollo received the territory from the French king. This became the **Duchy of Normandy**. The Normans soon adopted the French language and the Christian faith.

Duke **William** of Normandy won the **Battle of Hastings** in **1066** and became King of England. That is why he is called **William the Conqueror**. The **Bayeux Tapestry** tells this story like a long strip of pictures. It is about 70 metres long and almost 1000 years old. Today you can see it in the museum in Bayeux.

In the Second World War France was occupied by Germany. On **6 June 1944** Allied troops from the USA, Great Britain, Canada and other countries landed on five beaches in Normandy. This day is called **D-Day**. It was the start of the **liberation of western Europe**. Today museums and cemeteries on the coast recall this time.

Normandy has many meadows and cows. It is famous for **butter**, **cream** and cheeses such as **Camembert**, which is named after a village. **Apples** also grow here in great numbers. From them people make **cider**, an apple wine, and the apple brandy **Calvados**.

The painter **Claude Monet** lived from 1883 in **Giverny**. There he laid out a garden with a **water lily pond**, which he painted in many large pictures. On the coast at **Étretat** stand tall white **chalk cliffs**. Also very well known is **Mont-Saint-Michel**, a monastery mountain in the sea on the border with Brittany.

gewusst: At high tide Mont-Saint-Michel is almost completely surrounded by water.
Because the Normans conquered England, many French words came into the English language.

teile.einleitung: A peninsula is a piece of land that is surrounded by water on three sides and joined to the mainland on only one side. Europe has especially many peninsulas, large and small. Some experts even call Europe itself a great peninsula of Asia.
wichtigste: The Scandinavian Peninsula is the largest peninsula in Europe.
Norway, Sweden and part of Finland lie on it.
The Balkan Peninsula in the south-east is named after the Balkan Mountains in Bulgaria.
The Peloponnese forms the south of the Greek mainland.
The port city of Murmansk lies on the Kola Peninsula in Russia.
Chalkidiki has three headlands that stick out into the sea like fingers.
The Amalfi Coast lies on the Sorrentine Peninsula near Naples.

abschnitte.text: The word says it already: a peninsula is almost an island. It is surrounded by sea on three sides, but joined to the mainland on the fourth. The link can be very wide or just a narrow **isthmus**. Europe has a strongly indented coast with many bays and peninsulas. That is why the sea is not very far away from almost anywhere in Europe.

The **Scandinavian Peninsula** is the largest peninsula in Europe. Norway, Sweden and the north-west of Finland lie on it. In the west, the Scandes, a long mountain range, run along the coast. Further east lies the **Kola Peninsula** in Russia, between the Barents Sea and the White Sea. Its largest city is the port city of **Murmansk**. Denmark lies largely on the peninsula of **Jutland**.

abschnitte.titel: The three great peninsulas in the south
abschnitte.text: In the south, three large peninsulas stick out into the Mediterranean. Right in the west lies the **Iberian Peninsula**, with Spain and Portugal. In the middle lies the **Apennine Peninsula**, which looks like a boot and belongs for the most part to Italy. In the south-east lies the **Balkan Peninsula**, between the Adriatic, the Aegean and the Black Sea. It includes Greece, Albania and Bulgaria, among others. Its name comes from the Balkan Mountains in Bulgaria.

In Greece there are several well-known peninsulas. The **Peloponnese** forms the southernmost part of the mainland and is joined to the rest only by a narrow isthmus. **Chalkidiki** in the north has three fingers: Kassandra, Sithonia and Athos. Many old monasteries stand on Athos. Near Naples lies the **Sorrentine Peninsula**. It separates the Gulf of Naples from the Gulf of Salerno, and on its south side lies the famous Amalfi Coast.

There are also many peninsulas on the Atlantic. In the south-west of England, **Cornwall** sticks far out into the sea. It ends at **Land's End**, the westernmost point of England. In France, **Brittany** is a large peninsula with rocky coasts. On coasts like these, many people have always made their living from fishing and seafaring.

gewusst: At the end of the 19th century the Corinth Canal was dug through the isthmus of the Peloponnese. Even so, the Peloponnese is still called a peninsula.
As a landlocked country, Switzerland has no sea coast, but there are small peninsulas in its lakes, for example the Au on Lake Zurich.

teile.einleitung: London is the capital of Great Britain and lies on the Thames. The city is famous for red double-decker buses, the oldest underground railway in the world and Buckingham Palace.
wichtigste: London is the capital of the United Kingdom and lies on the Thames.
Around AD 50 the Romans founded the settlement of Londinium.
In 2024 about 9 million people lived in London.
The underground is called the “Tube” and has run since 1863.
Buckingham Palace has been the seat of the British monarchs since 1837.
People pay with the British pound.

abschnitte.text: Around the year AD 50 the **Romans** founded a settlement on the Thames called **Londinium**. Over the centuries a large trading city grew from it. In 1666 a great fire destroyed large parts of the city, and afterwards it was rebuilt. In 2024 about 9 million people lived in London, roughly as many as in the whole of Switzerland.

London has the **oldest underground railway in the world**. It opened in 1863. Londoners call it the **Tube**, because many of the tunnels are round. Also famous are the **red double-decker buses**. If you sit at the front on the top deck, you get a great view. Also red are the old **telephone boxes**, some of which now stand only as souvenirs.

**Buckingham Palace** has been the official seat of the British monarchs in London since 1837. In front of it the well-known changing of the guard takes place. On the bank of the Thames stands Parliament with the tower in which the great bell **Big Ben** hangs. The **Tower of London** is an old fortress in which the Crown Jewels are kept. Next to it, **Tower Bridge** crosses the river.

In the middle of the city lies **Hyde Park**, one of the largest parks in London. There you can stroll, have a picnic and go boating on a lake. On the Thames the giant wheel **London Eye** turns, about 135 metres high. From its capsules you can see far across the whole city.

In London people pay with the **British pound**, and the euro is not used there. Cars drive on the left-hand side of the road. In the district of **Greenwich** runs the prime meridian, from which the Earth's lines of longitude are counted. London has already hosted the Summer Olympics three times: 1908, 1948 and 2012.

gewusst: The London Underground is older than the first cars.
In Greenwich you can stand with one foot in the eastern and the other in the western half of the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Peberholm is an artificial island in the Øresund between Denmark and Sweden. It was built for the Øresund link, which connects Copenhagen and Malmö.
wichtigste: Peberholm is an artificial island that was built up from fill.
It belongs to Denmark.
On Peberholm the Øresund link changes from the bridge to the tunnel.
The Øresund link opened in 2000.
The name means roughly “Pepper Islet”.

abschnitte.text: The **Øresund link** connects **Copenhagen** in Denmark with **Malmö** in Sweden. It opened in the year **2000**. Cars and trains travel on it. From Sweden a long **bridge** leads over the sea. On the island of **Peberholm** the route dives into a **tunnel**. This runs under the sea to Denmark, near Copenhagen Airport.

A continuous bridge would have stood close to Copenhagen Airport. Tall bridge piers would have interfered with the **aircraft**. Ships also need enough room. That is why part of it was built as a tunnel. For the transition between bridge and tunnel, **Peberholm** was **built up** from stones and sand from the sea floor. The island is about 4 kilometres long.

The name **Peberholm** means roughly “Pepper Islet”. It matches the neighbouring island of **Saltholm**, the “Salt Islet”. No plants were planted on Peberholm. Researchers observe how **plants** and **animals** settle by themselves. That is why people are normally not allowed on the island.

gewusst: Hundreds of plant species have already settled by themselves on Peberholm.
The Øresund Bridge also became known abroad through a television series.

teile.einleitung: Malta is a small island state in the Mediterranean, south of Sicily. It is the smallest country in the European Union and has a very long and rich history.
wichtigste: At about 316 square kilometres, Malta is the smallest country in the EU.
The capital is called Valletta and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The second largest island is Gozo.
The official languages are Maltese and English.
Malta became independent from Britain in 1964 and has been in the EU since 2004.
The stone temples on Malta are older than the pyramids in Egypt.

abschnitte.text: The state of Malta consists of several islands. The largest is also called **Malta**, the second largest is **Gozo**, and between them lies the small island of Comino. Together they are only about **316 square kilometres** in size, a little larger than the canton of Schaffhausen. In 2024 about half a million people lived in the country, so they live very close together.

On Malta stand **stone temples** that are over 5000 years old. They are older than the pyramids in Egypt and are among the oldest freestanding buildings in the world. Who built them is known only roughly: they were people of the Neolithic who lived on the islands. The temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

From the 16th century a Christian order of knights ruled Malta, the **Knights of St John**, later called the **Knights of Malta**. Their sign is the **Maltese cross** with four arms and eight points. The knights built the capital, **Valletta**, with thick fortress walls. Today the whole old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

From 1814 Malta was a **British colony**. In **1964** the country became independent. It dates from the British period that people on Malta still drive on the **left** today. **English** also remained an official language alongside **Maltese**. Maltese is a Semitic language, so related to Arabic, but is written in Latin letters.

In **2004** Malta joined the **European Union** together with nine other states. Since 2008 people there have paid with the **euro**. Because of the warm climate, the clear water and the many language schools, many visitors come every year, including from Switzerland, to learn English.

gewusst: Maltese is the only Semitic language that is an official language of the EU.
Valletta is one of the smallest capitals in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Channel Islands are a group of islands in the English Channel off the coast of Normandy in France. Although they lie close to France, they belong to the British Crown. The best-known islands are Jersey and Guernsey.
wichtigste: The Channel Islands lie in the English Channel off Normandy.
The largest islands are Jersey and Guernsey.
They belong to the British Crown, but not to the United Kingdom.
The islands manage many things themselves, such as taxes and laws.
In the Second World War they were occupied by Germany.

abschnitte.text: The islands lie in the **English Channel**, the sea between England and France, close to the French coast. The largest islands are **Jersey** and **Guernsey**. Smaller islands such as Alderney and Sark also belong to Guernsey. There are strong tides there, and at low tide the sea draws back a long way.

The Channel Islands used to be part of the Duchy of **Normandy**. When the Duke of Normandy became King of England in 1066, they came to the English Crown. Today Jersey and Guernsey are so-called **Crown dependencies**. They do not belong to the United Kingdom, have their own parliaments and make many laws themselves. Great Britain, however, is responsible for defence and foreign policy.

On the islands people mainly speak English, but many place and street names are French. Banks and **tourism** are important today. The cattle breeds **Jersey** and **Guernsey**, whose milk contains an especially large amount of fat, are also well known. In the Second World War the islands were the only British soil occupied by German troops.

gewusst: Cars are banned on the small island of Sark, and people get around by bicycle, horse-drawn carriage or tractor.
Jersey and Guernsey issue their own banknotes and stamps.

teile.einleitung: Jutland is the mainland part of Denmark. It forms the northern part of a peninsula between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. The landscape is flat and windy and shaped by sand, heath and coasts.
wichtigste: Jutland is the northern part of the Cimbrian Peninsula, and the southern part belongs to Schleswig-Holstein.
The Limfjord separates the north of Jutland from the rest of the peninsula.
At the tip of Grenen near Skagen, the Skagerrak and the Kattegat meet.
Ribe is regarded as the oldest town in Denmark.
Aarhus is the largest city in Jutland and the second largest in Denmark.
Northern Schleswig came to Denmark in 1920 through a referendum.

abschnitte.text: Jutland sticks north like a finger between the **North Sea** in the west and the Baltic Sea in the east. In geography the whole peninsula is called the **Cimbrian Peninsula**, after the ancient people of the Cimbri. Its southern part belongs to the German federal state of Schleswig-Holstein. The northern part is Danish Jutland, the only piece of Denmark that is joined to the European mainland.

The **Limfjord** is a long arm of the sea that reaches right across northern Jutland. Since a storm surge in the 19th century it has linked the North Sea with the Kattegat. That is why the northernmost part is, strictly speaking, an island. In the far north lies the headland of **Grenen** near Skagen. There you can watch the waves of the **Skagerrak** and the **Kattegat** crash into each other.

In the Ice Age the ice covered only the east of Jutland. In front of the edge of the ice, **meltwater rivers** in the west laid down large areas of sand and gravel. These areas are called **sandar**. On the poor soils, heath mainly used to grow. On the west coast there are also high dunes and the Wadden Sea.

**Ribe** on the west coast arose in the early 8th century as a trading place of the Viking Age and is regarded as the oldest town in Denmark. **Aarhus** on the east coast is the largest city in Jutland, with a large university and an important port. **Esbjerg** was newly founded in 1868, because in 1864 Denmark had lost Schleswig and with it its western port. Today Esbjerg is a centre of offshore wind power.

After the **Second Schleswig War** of 1864, Denmark had to give up Schleswig. After the First World War, the **Treaty of Versailles** provided for votes in Schleswig. In 1920 the northern part voted by a majority for Denmark. That is how the present border between Germany and Denmark came about.

gewusst: The toy company LEGO comes from Billund in Jutland, and the first Legoland is there too.
Because of the special light in Skagen, many painters came there in the 19th century, and they are called the Skagen Painters.

teile.einleitung: Hvar is a long, narrow island in Dalmatia, off the coast of Croatia in the Adriatic. It is regarded as one of the sunniest islands in the country and is known for its lavender fields. Its history goes back to the time of the ancient Greeks.
wichtigste: Hvar is an island in Dalmatia in Croatia.
It is regarded as one of the sunniest islands in Croatia.
Lavender has been grown on Hvar for a long time.
The ancient Greeks founded a settlement here.
The Stari Grad Plain is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Hvar has many hours of sunshine a year and mild winters. That is why plants that love warmth grow here, such as olives, grapevines and **lavender**. The lavender blooms in early summer and turns whole slopes purple. Fragrant **lavender oil** is made from the flowers. Little bags of dried flowers are a popular souvenir.

In the 4th century BC, Greek settlers founded the town of **Pharos** on the island, which is now **Stari Grad**. They divided the fertile plain next to it into regular fields marked off by stone walls. This layout can still be seen today, which is why the **Stari Grad Plain** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Later Hvar belonged for a long time to the Republic of **Venice**, which many buildings still tell of.

The town of **Hvar**, which has the same name, lies on a sheltered bay. Above it towers an old **fortress**, from which you can see far over the sea and the islands lying off the coast. On the main square stands a building with one of the oldest public **theatres** in Europe, from the early 17th century. In summer many holidaymakers and sailing boats come to the island.

gewusst: The Greek fields near Stari Grad have been farmed for about 2400 years.

teile.einleitung: The Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands is the largest seaport in Europe. It lies where the Rhine and the Meuse flow into the North Sea. It is also important for Switzerland, because many goods travel from here by ship as far as Basel.
wichtigste: Rotterdam is the largest seaport in Europe.
More than 400 million tonnes of goods are handled there every year.
The port lies in the estuary of the Rhine and the Meuse.
The port extension Maasvlakte 2, on reclaimed land, opened in 2013.
Rhine ships carry goods from Rotterdam to the Rhine ports of Basel.
The second largest port in Europe is Antwerp in Belgium.

abschnitte.text: Every year, more than **400 million tonnes** of goods are handled in the **Port of Rotterdam**. No other port in Europe reaches this amount. Until **2004** Rotterdam was even the largest port in the world. Since then it has been overtaken by ports in **Asia** such as Shanghai and Singapore, which have grown strongly thanks to world trade. The second largest port in Europe is **Antwerp** in Belgium, which has been merged with Bruges since 2022.

Rotterdam lies in the shared estuary of the **Rhine** and the **Meuse**. As a result, ships are directly connected with the **hinterland**. The **Nieuwe Waterweg**, dug in the 19th century, links the city directly with the **North Sea**. For **Maasvlakte 2**, sand was pumped into the North Sea to gain new land. This extension opened in **2013**. The largest container ships dock there.

Goods from all over the world arrive in the port, many of them in **containers**. **Oil** is especially important: Rotterdam is a centre of the oil industry, with several **refineries** where crude oil is processed into petrol, diesel and other products. The **Port of Rotterdam Authority** manages the site and rents out areas to companies. About 70 per cent of it belongs to the **municipality of Rotterdam** and about 30 per cent to the Dutch state.

Switzerland has no sea coast. Even so, it is connected to the sea by the **Rhine**. **Rhine ships** carry goods such as containers and fuel from Rotterdam to the **Rhine ports of Basel**. In the other direction, Swiss goods also go out into the world this way. So Rotterdam is an important access to the sea for the Swiss economy.

gewusst: Part of the Port of Rotterdam stands on land that did not exist at all a few years ago.
A Rhine ship needs several days to get from Rotterdam to Basel, because it travels against the current.

teile.einleitung: The Mediterranean climate has hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. It prevails around the Mediterranean and shapes plants such as the olive tree.
wichtigste: In summer it is hot and dry.
Most of the rain falls in the winter half of the year.
The olive tree is regarded as the characteristic plant of the Mediterranean climate.
Many plants have hard, leathery leaves against drying out.
In summer the danger of forest fires is great.
Well-known winds are the mistral and the sirocco.

abschnitte.text: In summer the Mediterranean region is under the influence of **high-pressure areas**. Then it is **hot and dry**, and often it does not rain for weeks. In the **winter half of the year**, **low-pressure areas** move across the Mediterranean and bring most of the rain. Winters are mild, and frost is rare on the coast. This climate is also found in California, Chile, South Africa and Australia.

The **olive tree** is regarded as the **characteristic plant** of the Mediterranean climate. It tolerates hot, dry summers, but not hard frost. That is why its distribution shows fairly exactly where this climate prevails. Since antiquity people around the Mediterranean have grown olives, as well as wine, citrus fruits and grain.

Many plants have small, hard and leathery leaves. They are called **sclerophyllous plants**. Their tough leaves protect them from too much **evaporation** in summer. Where forests once stood, the **maquis** often grows today, a dense, evergreen scrub of myrtle, broom, rockroses and other shrubs.

After the long, dry summer many plants are parched. Then a single spark can set off a large **forest fire**. Strong wind fans the fire further. That is why strict rules apply in many Mediterranean countries in summer, for example bans on open fires.

The **mistral** is a cold, dry north wind that blows through the Rhône Valley to the Gulf of Lion. The **sirocco**, on the other hand, brings hot, often dusty air from the Sahara to southern Europe. Sometimes it even carries **Saharan dust** as far as Switzerland, and then the sky turns yellowish and fine dust lies on cars. In Ticino palm trees do grow, but it also rains a lot there in summer, which is why it is not a true Mediterranean climate.

gewusst: The Saharan dust that the sirocco brings sometimes colours the snow in the Swiss Alps reddish.
Olive trees can live to be many hundreds of years old.

teile.einleitung: Every year many people from Africa and Asia try to reach Europe across the Mediterranean. The crossings are dangerous, and how Europe should deal with this is strongly debated in politics.
wichtigste: The central Mediterranean route leads mainly from Libya and Tunisia to Italy and Malta.
The eastern route leads from Turkey to Greek islands such as Lesbos.
In 2015, according to UNHCR, over a million people came to Europe across the Mediterranean.
The central route is regarded as the deadliest known migration route in the world.
Under the Dublin rules, the state of first entry is usually responsible for the asylum procedure.
In May 2022 Switzerland voted Yes to expanding its participation in Frontex.

abschnitte.text: On the **central Mediterranean route** boats travel mainly from **Libya** and **Tunisia** to Italy, for example to **Lampedusa** and Sicily, or to Malta. The International Organization for Migration describes it as the **deadliest known migration route** in the world. On the **eastern route** people go from Turkey to Greek islands such as **Lesbos**. The distance is short, but the boats are often overcrowded. Another dangerous route is the **Atlantic route** from West Africa to the **Canary Islands**.

In **2015**, according to the UN refugee agency **UNHCR**, over a million people reached Europe by sea. Most arrived in Greece, and many were fleeing the war in **Syria**. From March 2016 the **EU-Turkey statement** was meant to reduce the crossings. Turkey undertook to take back migrants who had reached Greece irregularly. The EU promised, among other things, billions in aid for refugees in Turkey.

On 3 October 2013 a boat sank off Lampedusa, and over 360 people lost their lives. Afterwards Italy launched the naval operation **Mare Nostrum**, which for a year rescued tens of thousands of people from distress at sea. At the end of 2014 it was replaced by the smaller EU operation **Triton**. Today, besides states, private aid organisations also rescue people at sea.

Under the **Dublin Regulation**, the state in which someone first entered is usually responsible for an asylum procedure. Because many people arrive first in Italy, Greece, Malta or Spain, these countries are particularly burdened. The Spanish cities of **Ceuta** and **Melilla** on the coast of North Africa are secured by high border fences. The EU border protection agency is called **Frontex**.

Switzerland is not an EU member, but applies Schengen and Dublin as an associated state. On **15 May 2022** the people voted by about **71.5 per cent** in favour of expanding participation in Frontex. A No could have endangered Swiss membership of Schengen. In politics there are different views: some call for more **sea rescue** and safe escape routes, others for stronger **border protection** and fewer irregular entries.

gewusst: The island of Lampedusa lies closer to Africa than to the Italian mainland.
Between Turkey and some Greek islands there are only a few kilometres of sea at the narrowest point.

teile.einleitung: The lavvu is the traditional tent of the Sámi in the far north of Europe. It is shaped like a cone and can be put up and taken down quickly. That was practical for life with the reindeer.
wichtigste: The lavvu is the traditional tent of the Sámi.
It is cone-shaped and consists of poles and a cover.
It can be put up and taken down quickly.
In the middle a fire often burns, and the smoke escapes at the top.
It was practical when travelling with the reindeer herds.

abschnitte.text: A lavvu consists of several **wooden poles** that meet at the top. A **cover** is laid over them. This creates a **cone-shaped** tent. In the past the covering was made of skins or other natural materials, today mostly of strong fabric. A lavvu looks similar to a tipi, but is often lower and therefore stable in wind.

abschnitte.titel: On the move with the reindeer
abschnitte.text: The **Sámi** live in **Lapland**, in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. Many of them keep **reindeer**. In the past they moved with the herds back and forth between summer and winter pastures. For this they needed a tent that could be **put up and taken down quickly** and easily carried along. The lavvu was ideal for that.

In the middle of the lavvu a **fire** often burns. It gives warmth and is used for cooking. The smoke escapes through the opening at the top. Around the fire people sit and sleep on skins and branches. Today the Sámi still use the lavvu for reindeer work, at festivals and in tourism.

gewusst: Because the lavvu is so low and round, it also stands up to strong wind in the open landscape of the north.

teile.einleitung: The High Tatras are the highest part of the Carpathians. The mountains lie on the border between Slovakia and Poland. With their pointed granite peaks, clear mountain lakes and national parks, they look like a small piece of the Alps.
wichtigste: The High Tatras lie in Slovakia and in Poland.
Their highest peak is Gerlachovský štít, about 2655 metres high.
The highest point in Poland lies on Rysy.
About two thirds of the area belongs to Slovakia.
The mountains consist mostly of granite.
The Slovak national park TANAP was founded in 1949.
Kriváň is shown on Slovak euro coins.

abschnitte.titel: The highest mountains of the Carpathians
abschnitte.text: The **Carpathians** stretch in a great arc through eastern Europe. Their highest part is the **High Tatras**. They cover about 340 square kilometres, so a comparatively small area. About **two thirds** lie in Slovakia and one third in Poland. The highest peak is **Gerlachovský štít** at about 2655 metres. Because no marked hiking trail leads up it, most visitors climb it with a mountain guide.

The High Tatras consist mostly of **granite**. This rock solidified about 315 million years ago, deep in the Earth. Only much later was it lifted upwards. In the ice ages **glaciers** shaped the valleys and carved sharp ridges and peaks. When the ice melted, many **mountain lakes** were left behind in the hollows.

On the border lie the **Rysy**. On the north-western summit, at about 2499 metres, is the highest point in Poland, while the main summit belongs to Slovakia. Below lies the lake **Morskie Oko**, which means “eye of the sea”. It is a popular destination near the town of **Zakopane**. On the Slovak side mountain lakes are usually called “**pleso**”, for example the Štrbské pleso, and on the Polish side often “staw”.

abschnitte.titel: National parks and the great storm
abschnitte.text: The Slovak **Tatra National Park TANAP** was founded in 1949 and is the oldest national park in Slovakia. On the Polish side the Tatra National Park TPN followed in 1954. Chamois, marmots and brown bears live here. On 19 November 2004 a **hurricane-force storm** swept across the southern side of the Tatras. On about 12,000 hectares it knocked down almost half of the trees. Since then the forest has been slowly growing back.

A **cable car** leads up **Lomnický štít**, the Lomnica Peak, at about 2632 metres. On the summit stand a weather station and an observatory. **Kriváň**, with its curved peak, is about 2494 metres high. It is regarded as a national symbol of Slovakia and is shown on the Slovak 1, 2 and 5 cent coins.

gewusst: Gerlachovský štít is the highest mountain in the whole of the Carpathians, although they stretch across several countries.
The name Morskie Oko comes from an old legend according to which the lake is joined to the sea underground.

teile.einleitung: Nord Stream is the name of two natural gas pipelines that run through the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany. They were politically controversial and were badly damaged by explosions in 2022.
wichtigste: Nord Stream 1 runs about 1224 kilometres from Vyborg in Russia to Lubmin near Greifswald.
The first line went into operation in November 2011, and the second in 2012.
The pipelines were meant to bring gas to Germany without transit countries.
The operating companies were based in the canton of Zug.
In February 2022 Germany stopped the certification of Nord Stream 2.
In September 2022 three of the four lines were destroyed by explosions near Bornholm.

abschnitte.text: A **pipeline** is a long pipe through which, for example, **natural gas** flows. **Nord Stream 1** begins at **Vyborg** near the Finnish border in Russia. It runs about **1224 kilometres** over the floor of the **Baltic Sea** to Germany. Both pipeline systems end at **Lubmin near Greifswald** in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From there the gas was passed on into the European network.

The first line of Nord Stream 1 went into operation in **November 2011**, and the second in **October 2012**. Each system consists of two lines and was designed for **55 billion cubic metres** of gas a year. Later **Nord Stream 2** was built, which was meant to double the amount. The operating companies **Nord Stream AG** and **Nord Stream 2 AG** were based in **Zug**. The majority owner was the Russian group **Gazprom**.

From the operators' point of view, gas was to flow directly to Germany without **transit countries**. Transit countries are countries through which a pipeline runs, such as **Ukraine**, **Poland** and **Belarus**. These countries and other states criticised the project. They feared that Europe would become too dependent on Russian gas. Supporters, on the other hand, stressed a secure and affordable supply.

On **22 February 2022** Chancellor **Olaf Scholz** stopped the approval procedure for Nord Stream 2. This was a reaction to Russia's actions against **Ukraine**. The fully built pipeline therefore **never went into operation**. The Nord Stream 2 AG in Zug then fell into severe financial difficulty.

On **26 September 2022** large leaks were discovered in the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of **Bornholm**. They had been caused by **explosions**. Both lines of Nord Stream 1 and one line of Nord Stream 2 were destroyed. The sites lay partly in Danish and partly in Swedish waters. Who is responsible has been investigated for a long time by several countries.

gewusst: On the sea surface above the leaks the escaping gas bubbled up in large circles that could be seen from the air.
The Nord Stream pipes lie on the sea floor and are encased in a thick layer of concrete.

teile.einleitung: Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic, just below the Arctic Circle. It was formed by volcanoes and at the same time has huge glaciers. That is why Iceland is often called the “land of fire and ice”.
wichtigste: Iceland is a volcanic island in the North Atlantic.
The capital Reykjavík is the northernmost capital of an independent state.
The word geyser comes from Iceland.
The largest glacier is Vatnajökull.
In 2010 the volcano Eyjafjallajökull brought air traffic in Europe to a standstill.
Many houses are heated with hot water from the ground.
Iceland is about two and a half times as large as Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Iceland lies exactly on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**. There two great plates of the Earth's crust are slowly drifting apart, the North American and the Eurasian plate. Liquid rock rises through the gaps. In this way Iceland grew out of the sea through **volcanic eruptions**. Even today there are many active **volcanoes**. In 2010 **Eyjafjallajökull** erupted. Its ash cloud drifted over Europe, and many aeroplanes had to stay on the ground for days.

Besides the volcanoes, Iceland has large **glaciers**. The largest is **Vatnajökull**, and there are even volcanoes under its ice. Because there is both hot lava and thick ice, people speak of the “land of fire and ice”. Iceland covers about 103,000 square kilometres, and Switzerland about 41,000. Iceland is therefore about **two and a half times** as large, but has far fewer inhabitants, fewer than 400,000 (as of 2023).

A **geyser** is a hot spring that again and again shoots water high into the air. The word comes from Iceland, from the “Great Geysir” in the south-west. Today **Strokkur** nearby is the most active: it shoots a column of water into the air every few minutes. Beneath Iceland the Earth is very hot. That is why many houses are heated with **hot water from the ground**. This heat is called **geothermal energy**.

The capital **Reykjavík** is the northernmost capital of an independent state. A large share of Iceland's people live here. Its name means “smoky bay”, because of the steam from hot springs. Iceland has a very old parliament, the **Althing**. It was founded in the year 930 and used to meet in the open air at Thingvellir.

The **Icelandic horse** is small and strong. It has a special gait, the **tölt**. In it the horse moves quickly and very smoothly, so the rider is hardly shaken at all. There are also many Icelandic horses in Switzerland. Millions of **puffins** breed on Iceland's cliffs. These birds have a colourful beak and dive skilfully for fish.

gewusst: In Iceland an Icelandic horse that has once left the country may not be brought back, so that no diseases are brought in.
In summer it hardly gets dark in Iceland, while in winter it is light for only a few hours.

teile.einleitung: Kiruna is a mining town in Lapland in the far north of Sweden. Beneath the town lies one of the largest iron ore mines in the world. Because the ground is sinking as a result of the mining, the town centre is being moved to a new site.
wichtigste: Kiruna lies north of the Arctic Circle and is the northernmost town in Sweden.
The state-owned company LKAB runs the largest underground iron ore mine in the world.
The main mineral mined is the magnetic ore mineral magnetite.
Because the ground is sinking, the centre is being moved about 3 kilometres to the east.
The new town centre opened in 2022.
Much of the ore is carried by the ore railway to the ice-free port of Narvik in Norway.
In 2023 LKAB reported the largest known deposit of rare earths in Europe.

abschnitte.text: Mining began in **1898**, at first as an **open-cast mine** and later moved underground. The mine in the mountain **Kiirunavaara** belongs to the Swedish state company **LKAB** and is the largest underground iron ore mine in the world. The main mineral mined is **magnetite**, a strongly magnetic iron oxide. In 2020 the main level lay about 1365 metres deep. The ore is processed into small balls, **pellets**, and delivered to steelworks.

The mining under the town leads to **ground movements** and cracks. That is why the centre of Kiruna is being moved about 3 kilometres to the east. Homes, schools and the town hall are being built anew. Some old buildings, such as the well-known wooden church, are even being moved in one piece. The new town centre opened in 2022.

Since 1902 the **ore railway** has linked Kiruna with **Narvik** in Norway. Thanks to the warm **Gulf Stream**, the port of Narvik is ice-free all year round. The Swedish port of Luleå on the Baltic Sea, on the other hand, freezes over in winter. In the **Second World War** the ore was an important raw material for the German war effort. The fighting for Narvik in 1940 was also connected with these deliveries.

In the **HYBRIT** project, SSAB, LKAB and Vattenfall are working together. They want to make steel from Kiruna ore using **hydrogen** instead of coal. This produces almost no CO2. In January 2023 LKAB also reported the largest known deposit of **rare earths** in Europe in the region. These metals are needed for electric motors and wind turbines, for example.

gewusst: Near Kiruna lies the village of Jukkasjärvi, which builds a hotel entirely of ice every winter.
In winter you can often see the northern lights in Kiruna.

teile.einleitung: Moscow is the capital of Russia and one of the largest cities in Europe. The Kremlin, magnificent metro stations and the Bolshoi Theatre are well known.
wichtigste: Moscow is the capital of Russia.
Through the city flows the Moskva, after which Moscow is named.
Moscow is first mentioned in a chronicle in 1147.
The first metro line opened in 1935.
The Bolshoi Theatre is famous for ballet and opera.
The city plan is radial-concentric: streets lead outward from the Kremlin like rays, and rings cross them.

abschnitte.text: Moscow is first mentioned in a chronicle in the year **1147**, in connection with Prince **Yuri Dolgorukiy**. This year is regarded as its founding year. In the centre stands the **Kremlin**, a fortress with red walls, towers and churches. Next to it lies **Red Square** with the colourful **Saint Basil's Cathedral**. Moscow is the capital of **Russia**, the largest country in the world.

The **Moskva** river flows through the city and gave it its name. The city plan is **radial-concentric**: from the Kremlin great streets lead outward like rays. Several rings cross them, for example the Boulevard Ring and the Garden Ring. Right on the outside lies the **MKAD** ring motorway, about **109 kilometres** long, which for a long time counted as the city boundary.

The **Moscow Metro** opened in **1935**. Many stations look like **palaces** with chandeliers, marble and colourful pictures. In the time of the **Soviet Union** they were meant to show, as “palaces for the people”, how strong the state was. Today millions of people ride the metro every day.

Under **Stalin**, seven large tall buildings in an ornate wedding-cake style were built between **1947** and **1957**. They are called the **Seven Sisters**. The largest is the main building of **Lomonosov University**. West of the centre the modern district of **Moscow City** was built, with some of the tallest buildings in Europe.

The **Bolshoi Theatre** is one of the best-known theatres in the world for **ballet** and **opera**. “Bolshoi” means **“big”** in Russian. Moscow also has many museums, for example the Tretyakov Gallery with Russian art. Famous composers such as Tchaikovsky also worked in the city.

gewusst: Some Moscow metro stations lie so deep underground that the escalators take several minutes.
The word Kremlin means roughly “fortress” in Russian; other Russian cities also have a kremlin.

teile.einleitung: Lithuania is the southernmost of the three Baltic states on the Baltic Sea. The capital is Vilnius. In 1990 Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare its independence.
wichtigste: Lithuania is the southernmost Baltic state and borders Poland and Belarus.
The capital is Vilnius, and the second largest city is Kaunas.
On 11 March 1990 Lithuania declared its independence.
Klaipėda, formerly Memel, is the only large seaport.
The island castle of Trakai lies in Lake Galvė, west of Vilnius.
Lithuanian is regarded as a particularly archaic Indo-European language.

abschnitte.text: **Lithuania** is the southernmost of the three **Baltic states**. It borders Latvia, **Poland**, **Belarus** and the Russian region of Kaliningrad. The capital is **Vilnius**. The port city of **Klaipėda**, formerly **Memel**, is the only large seaport on the Baltic Sea. Part of the **Curonian Spit** also belongs to Lithuania.

In the Middle Ages Lithuania was a powerful **grand duchy**. The island castle of **Trakai** in **Lake Galvė**, west of Vilnius, was a residence of the grand dukes. It dates from the 14th and 15th centuries and was rebuilt from ruins in the 20th century. With the **Union of Lublin** in 1569 Poland and Lithuania joined to form one state. It lasted until the **partitions of Poland** at the end of the 18th century.

From **1920 to 1939** **Kaunas** was the **temporary capital** of Lithuania. In this period hundreds of modern buildings were built. This **modernist architecture** was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in **2023** as “Architecture of Optimism”. Today Kaunas is the second largest city in the country.

abschnitte.titel: Independence and the Hill of Crosses
abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Lithuania belonged to the **Soviet Union**. On **11 March 1990** it declared, as the **first Soviet republic**, the restoration of its **independence**. The Soviet Union only recognised this in September 1991. About 12 kilometres north of **Šiauliai** lies the **Hill of Crosses** with tens of thousands of crosses. The Soviet authorities had it levelled several times, but people kept putting up new crosses.

The **Lithuanian language** is regarded as a particularly **archaic Indo-European language**. It has preserved many old forms, such as many different **cases**. That is why it is very important to linguists. Lithuanian is written in **Latin letters**. Since 2004 Lithuania has belonged to the EU.

gewusst: On the Hill of Crosses there are so many crosses that nobody can count them exactly.
Lithuanian has preserved some word forms that recall the ancient Sanskrit.

teile.einleitung: The Caucasus is a high mountain range between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. It lies on the border between Europe and Asia. Its highest mountain is Elbrus.
wichtigste: The Caucasus stretches from the Black Sea in the west to the Caspian Sea in the east.
It consists of two chains: the higher Greater Caucasus in the north and the Lesser Caucasus in the south.
The highest mountain is Elbrus, about 5642 metres high.
Elbrus is a dormant volcano and lies in Russia.
Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan lie in the Caucasus region.
The highest peaks are covered with glaciers.

abschnitte.text: The Caucasus stretches from the **Black Sea** in the west to the **Caspian Sea** in the east. It consists of two mountain chains. In the north lies the higher **Greater Caucasus**, and in the south the **Lesser Caucasus**. Between them lie wide valleys and plains.

The highest mountain is **Elbrus**. Its western summit is about 5642 metres high, so much higher than Mont Blanc in the Alps. Elbrus is a **dormant volcano** with two summits that has not erupted for a long time. It lies in the north of the mountains in **Russia**. It is often described as the highest mountain in Europe, depending on where you draw the border with Asia.

Several mountains in the Caucasus are over 5000 metres high. Up there there is **snow** and there are **glaciers** all year round. Another well-known mountain is **Kazbek**, which is also a volcano. It lies on the border between Georgia and Russia and is about 5050 metres high.

The countries of **Georgia**, **Armenia** and **Azerbaijan** lie in the Caucasus region, and the north belongs to Russia. Very many different peoples with their own languages live here. The Georgian capital **Tbilisi** lies on the River Kura in a valley between the Greater and the Lesser Caucasus. Georgia is very mountainous and lies on the Black Sea.

gewusst: Dozens of different languages are spoken in the Caucasus in a small area.
Georgia is regarded as one of the oldest wine-growing countries in the world.

teile.einleitung: The martenitsa is a lucky band of red and white threads that people in Bulgaria wear from 1 March. It is meant to bring health and to welcome spring.
wichtigste: The martenitsa is a red and white band made of threads.
People give and wear it in Bulgaria from 1 March.
It is meant to bring health and luck.
People wear it until they see a stork or a blossoming tree.
Since 2017 the custom has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: A **martenitsa** consists of twisted red and white threads. Often they are small figures, tassels or bracelets. On **1 March** family, friends and classmates give each other martenitsi. People wear them on the wrist or on their clothes. White stands for purity, red for health and strength.

The custom is linked with a figure from folk tales: **Baba Marta**, which means Grandmother March. She is said to be moody, like the weather in March, which changes between sun and snow. With the martenitsi people want to put her in a good mood, so that winter ends and **spring** comes.

People wear the martenitsa until they see the first **stork** or a **blossoming tree**. Then they often hang it on a branch. In spring in Bulgaria you therefore see many trees with red and white bands. Similar customs exist in Romania, Moldova and North Macedonia. Since 2017 they have together been part of UNESCO's **intangible cultural heritage**.

gewusst: In spring some trees in Bulgaria carry so many martenitsi that they look decorated.

teile.einleitung: Karst is a landscape of limestone in which water slowly dissolves the rock. Typical features are caves, sinkholes and rivers that disappear into the ground. The name comes from a region in Slovenia.
wichtigste: The term comes from the Kras, a limestone plateau in the south-west of Slovenia.
Karst forms when rainwater dissolves limestone.
Typical features are caves, sinkholes and rivers that seep away.
Sinkholes are funnel-shaped dips in the ground.
There are also karst landscapes in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **Kras** is a limestone plateau in the south-west of **Slovenia**, close to Trieste. In German the area is called **Karst**. In the 19th century researchers studied the special forms of the landscape there. That is why the name was taken over for all similar landscapes in the world.

Rainwater takes up some **carbon dioxide** from the air and the soil and becomes slightly acidic. This water can slowly dissolve **limestone**. This creates cracks, underground passages and large **caves**. On the surface, funnel-shaped dips form, called **sinkholes** or **dolines**. Rivers often seep away into the ground and flow on underground.

There are also karst areas in Switzerland, for example in the **Jura** and in the limestone Alps. In the Muota valley in the canton of Schwyz lies the **Hölloch**, one of the longest cave systems in the world. On many limestone surfaces in the Alps you can see **karren**, which are grooves that the water has eaten into the rock. In Slovenia the **Postojna Cave** is world famous.

gewusst: The olm lives in Postojna Cave, a pale, almost blind amphibian that can live to a great age.
Stalactites and stalagmites often grow only a few millimetres in a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: France produces a large part of its electricity in nuclear power stations. Hardly any other large country relies so heavily on nuclear energy. Some plants lie close to the Swiss border.
wichtigste: At the end of 2024, 57 nuclear reactors were in operation in France.
Nuclear power supplies about two thirds of electricity in France (as of 2024).
With the Messmer Plan of 1974, France decided on a large expansion.
The state-owned company EDF operates all the reactors.
The Fessenheim nuclear power station near Basel was shut down in 2020.
In Flamanville the new EPR reactor started up for the first time in 2024.
In 2022 President Macron announced six new reactors.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 1970s oil suddenly became very expensive. France wanted to depend less on **oil imports**. Prime Minister **Pierre Messmer** therefore had a large expansion of nuclear power decided in 1974, the **Messmer Plan**. In the following 15 years dozens of reactors were built. Since then a large part of the electricity has come from nuclear power, in the past even over 70 per cent.

All the reactors are operated by the company **Électricité de France**, or **EDF** for short. In 2023 EDF was fully nationalised again. With 57 reactors at the end of 2024, France is one of the countries with the most reactors in the world. In 2022, more than half of the 56 reactors at the time were shut down for a while because of **corrosion** in pipes and maintenance work. France then had to import electricity on balance for the first time in decades.

**Fessenheim** in Alsace was the oldest French nuclear power station and lay about 40 kilometres from Basel. Its two reactors were shut down in 2020. The **Bugey** nuclear power station also lies not far from Geneva. At **La Hague** in Normandy, spent **fuel elements** are reprocessed: uranium and plutonium are recovered from them. In the past Switzerland also had fuel elements reprocessed there.

At **Flamanville** a new type of reactor was built, the **EPR** (European Pressurised Reactor). Construction began in 2007 and took about 17 years, and the costs rose sharply. In 2024 the reactor started up for the first time. In 2022 President Emmanuel Macron announced in Belfort the building of six new reactors of the type **EPR2**, with the option of eight more. The first sites are Penly, Gravelines and Bugey.

Supporters stress that nuclear power stations supply a lot of electricity and give off hardly any **CO2** in doing so. Critics point to the risk of accidents and to the **radioactive waste**, which has to be stored safely for a very long time. In Switzerland, too, the future of nuclear energy is discussed. Opinions on it differ in both countries.

gewusst: In normal years France sells a lot of electricity to neighbouring countries, including Switzerland.
Many French nuclear power stations stand on rivers, because they need a lot of water for cooling.

teile.einleitung: The Channel Tunnel, also called the Eurotunnel, links England and France under the sea. It runs under the English Channel and opened in 1994. Only trains travel through it.
wichtigste: The tunnel runs under the sea floor of the English Channel.
It opened in 1994.
It is about 50 kilometres long, and almost 38 kilometres of it lie under the sea.
It consists of three tubes: two for trains and one for emergencies and maintenance.
Cars travel on special trains that take them through the tunnel.
The high-speed Eurostar train links London and Paris.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland is even longer.

abschnitte.text: The tunnel lies deep under the sea floor of the **English Channel**. It begins in England near Folkestone and ends in France near Calais. Ships sail above it. The idea for a tunnel like this was around more than 200 years ago, but it was only realised at the end of the 20th century.

Building began in 1988, from both sides at the same time, using large **tunnel boring machines**. In 1990 the workers met in the middle. On 6 May 1994 the tunnel was officially opened. It consists of **three tubes**: two are for trains, one for each direction. In the middle lies a **service tunnel** for emergencies and maintenance.

Cars, buses and lorries do not drive through the tunnel themselves. They drive onto special train carriages, the so-called **shuttle**. People mostly stay sitting in their car. In about half an hour you are on the other side. In the past you could only get to England by ship or aeroplane.

The high-speed **Eurostar** train links **London** and **Paris** in a little over two hours. There are also connections to Brussels. The tunnel is about 50 kilometres long and so one of the longest railway tunnels in the world. Its section under the sea is the longest of any tunnel in the world.

Even longer is the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** in Switzerland. It is about 57 kilometres long and is regarded as the longest railway tunnel in the world. It opened in 2016 and leads through the Alps instead of under the sea. Both tunnels show how railways link countries more closely.

gewusst: So much rock was dug out when the Channel Tunnel was built that it was used to create new land by the sea in England.
At its deepest point the tunnel lies about 75 metres below sea level.

teile.einleitung: Austria is a federal state with nine federal states. Each Land has its own capital and its own government. Two of them, Vorarlberg and Tyrol, border Switzerland.
wichtigste: Austria has nine federal states.
Lower Austria is the largest federal state and surrounds Vienna.
Bregenz on Lake Constance is the capital of Vorarlberg.
Graz is the capital of Styria and the second largest city in Austria.
Burgenland was the last Land to join Austria, in 1921.
Linz is the capital of Upper Austria, and Klagenfurt that of Carinthia.

abschnitte.text: Austria consists of **nine federal states**: Vienna, Lower Austria, Upper Austria, Salzburg, Tyrol, Vorarlberg, Carinthia, Styria and Burgenland. Each Land has a **Landtag** (state parliament) and a state government. At its head stands the **Landeshauptmann** or the Landeshauptfrau, the state governor. **Vienna** is both the capital of Austria and a federal state of its own.

**Vorarlberg** is the westernmost federal state and borders Switzerland. Its capital **Bregenz** lies on the eastern shore of **Lake Constance**. The **Bregenz Festival**, held on the floating stage in the lake, is well known. **Tyrol**, with its capital Innsbruck, also borders Switzerland, namely the canton of Graubünden.

**Lower Austria**, at about **19,200 square kilometres**, is the largest federal state. It completely surrounds the capital **Vienna**. **Upper Austria** lies to the west of it. Its capital **Linz** on the **Danube** is an important centre of industry and culture.

**Graz** is the capital of **Styria** and the **second largest city** in Austria. It lies on the River Mur. The old town with the **Clock Tower** on the Schlossberg is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the south lies **Carinthia**, the southernmost federal state. Its capital is **Klagenfurt** on the Wörthersee, and its landmark is the **Lindwurm Fountain**.

**Burgenland** is the easternmost federal state. It used to belong to **Hungary** and only came to Austria in **1921**. That makes it the Land that joined last. Its capital is **Eisenstadt**. The landscape is flat, and a lot of wine is grown at Lake Neusiedl.

gewusst: At the Bregenz Festival the stage stands in the middle of Lake Constance.
Vienna is completely surrounded by Lower Austria.

teile.einleitung: The Meseta is the great plateau in the interior of Spain. It takes up a large part of the Iberian Peninsula and is known for wide fields, hot summers and cold winters.
wichtigste: The Meseta is the central plateau of the Iberian Peninsula.
It mostly lies at 600 to 800 metres above sea level.
The Central System divides it into the Northern and Southern Meseta.
The climate is continental, with hot summers and cold winters.
Traditionally grain is grown and sheep are kept.
In La Mancha stand the windmills from the novel about Don Quixote.

abschnitte.text: The **Meseta** is the extensive **plateau** in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula. The name means roughly “little table” and alludes to the flat, raised shape. Most of it lies at **600 to 800 metres** above sea level, so a little higher than the Swiss Plateau. The capital, **Madrid**, also lies on the Meseta.

The **Central System**, in Spanish Sistema Central, divides the Meseta into a northern and a southern half. The Sierra de Guadarrama north of Madrid belongs to it. Most of the **Northern Meseta** is drained by the River **Duero**. It flows west and at Porto flows into the Atlantic as the Douro. Through the Southern Meseta flow the Tagus and the Guadiana.

Mountains around the Meseta keep out the damp sea air. That is why there is a **continental climate**: summers are very hot and dry, and winters cold. It rains little. That is why people mainly grew **grain** such as wheat and barley without irrigation. This dry farming is called secano in Spanish. Alongside it there is wine growing.

For centuries **sheep farming** has shaped the Meseta, for example with **merino sheep**, whose wool is very fine. The powerful association of sheep breeders was called the **Mesta**. It was recognised by the Castilian king in 1273. Its flocks travelled over long distances every year between summer pastures in the north and winter pastures in the south. This migratory grazing is called **transhumance**.

On the southern Meseta lies the region of **La Mancha** with its white **windmills**. It became famous through the novel by **Miguel de Cervantes**. In it the knight **Don Quixote** fights windmills because he takes them for giants. To this day many visitors come to see the mills on the hills.

gewusst: Madrid is one of the highest capitals in Europe because it lies on the Meseta.
The old droving routes of the sheep flocks are still partly protected today, and sometimes flocks even move through Madrid.

teile.einleitung: The Lusatian lignite region lies in the east of Germany. Lignite, or brown coal, has been mined here for a long time in huge pits and burned in power stations. By 2038 at the latest this is due to end, and old pits will become lakes.
wichtigste: The region lies in Brandenburg and Saxony.
After the Rhenish region it is the second largest lignite region in Germany.
Since 2016 LEAG has run the open-cast mines and power stations.
Many villages of the Sorbs had to make way for the mining.
The Lusatian Lakeland is forming from old open-cast mines.
Germany wants to end coal power generation by 2038 at the latest.

abschnitte.text: The Lusatian region lies in the south-east of **Brandenburg** and the north-east of **Saxony**. After the **Rhenish region** it is the second largest lignite region in Germany. The coal is extracted by **open-cast mining**, that is, in open pits. Giant excavators first remove the earth above it. Vattenfall sold the business in 2016 to the Czech EPH group, and since then **LEAG** has run open-cast mines such as **Welzow-Süd** and **Nochten**.

Raw lignite often contains about **50 per cent water** and has a low **calorific value**. For the same amount of electricity, more of it must therefore be burned than of hard coal. This releases more **CO2** and harms the climate. The **Jänschwalde** power station near Peitz, close to the Polish border, is among the largest and most CO2-intensive power stations in Europe. Under the **Coal Phase-Out Act** of 2020, Germany is to generate no more electricity from coal by **2038** at the latest.

Lusatia is the home region of the **Sorbs**, a Slavic **minority** with a language of its own. In the 20th century dozens of villages disappeared for coal mining, many of them with a Sorbian character. The residents were **resettled**, that is, moved to another place. A well-known example is **Horno**, which had to make way in the early 2000s.

Closed open-cast mines are **flooded** with water. This is how the **Lusatian Lakeland** is forming, one of the largest artificial lake landscapes in Europe. Since 2019 the former **Cottbus-Nord** mine has been turning into the **Cottbus Baltic Sea** lake. It is meant to become one of the largest artificial lakes in Germany.
